First, that our offering to God must not be superficial: in the Old Testament sacrifice, the kidneys (precious, secret part) are offered in their entirety. Second, that God knows the inner workings of our heart far better than we do: we cannot deceive Him about our true intentions. Our kidneys — what truly motivates us — are always open to His gaze.

sens: Son of Elimelech and Naomi
Brother of Mahlon
Husband of Orpah or Ruth
Man from Ephrath who died in the land of Moab
H3630.detail: 1. Kiljon is one of the two sons of Elimelech and Naomi, originally from Bethlehem in Judah (Ruth 1:2). His name means "the one who pines away" or "consumption" in Hebrew, possibly evoking a fragile nature or a brief life. 2. He is the brother of Mahlon, both being children of the same couple (Ruth 1:2, 1:5). 3. According to Scripture, Kiljon was married: Jewish tradition says he married Orpah, while some ancient manuscripts list him as the husband of Ruth (Ruth 1:4). 4. Kiljon dies in the land of Moab shortly after arriving there with his family, leaving his wife a widow and his mother Naomi alone and unsupported (Ruth 1:5). His death has major consequences for Naomi's fate and the redemption plan that will follow.
H3630.origine: The name Kiljon (כִּלְיוֹן) comes from a Hebrew root expressing exhaustion, consumption, or debility — the idea of a life that is extinguished or weakened. It is a name that summarizes the brevity of his earthly existence: having come from the land of Israel seeking bread in Moab, he loses his life there without leaving descendants to perpetuate his name. This name, like that of his brother Mahlon ("sickness"), carries a dark and ominous tone.
H3630.emploi: Kiljon appears three times in the book of Ruth, always in the introductory narratives of the story (Ruth 1:2, 1:5, and 4:9). He is first mentioned as the son of Elimelech during the departure from Bethlehem to Moab (Ruth 1:2), then again when his death is announced after that of his father (Ruth 1:5), and finally in the legal act of land acquisition where Boaz recalls that these properties belonged to Kiljon and his family (Ruth 4:9). Although Kiljon dies without known offspring, his name remains inscribed in the redemption narrative that will lead to the birth of Obed, the grandfather of King David, through Ruth's remarriage (probably the widow of Kiljon or Mahlon) to Boaz.
H3630.portee: Kiljon represents the fragility of human life in the face of trials: arriving as a stranger in Moab in search of survival, he dies there without fulfilling his plans. His brief existence shows that human plans depend on God's will. Yet, his death is part of the path through which God will accomplish His redemption plan, transforming a family tragedy into a blessing for Naomi and, through Ruth, into a part of the lineage of the Messiah. This teaches the reader that even brief and seemingly insignificant lives are integrated into the divine plan.

sens: total annihilation, complete end
progressive consumption until exhaustion
weakening of the soul, loss of courage
H3631.detail: 1. Destruction is the final outcome of a process: it is total annihilation, the complete end of something. In Isaiah 10:22, God decrees a "resolved destruction" of Israel, an irrevocable decision of annihilation that cannot be stopped. 2. The word can also refer to a progressive consumption, the gradual exhaustion of a thing or a person. It is an end that unfolds rather than a sudden halt. 3. Figuratively, it describes the deep weakening of the soul, the withering of courage and vital strength: in Deuteronomy 28:65, God promises unfaithful Israel "a trembling heart, failing eyes, and a languishing soul" — it is this inner destruction, this exhaustion of the heart in the face of perpetual threat.
H3631.origine: The word comes from the root "kll" which means "to finish, to complete, to fill completely." The basic image is that of a measure filled to the brim: hence the idea of completeness that tips into annihilation. The same root produces the word "klilout" (perfection, totality), but turned towards the negative, it becomes destruction — the complete filling of misfortune, in a sense.
H3631.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Deuteronomy 28:65, it is found in the curse that God pronounces against Israel if it violates His covenant: the people will experience a destruction of the heart, a constant terror, and a languishing of the soul. In Isaiah 10:22, the prophet asserts that despite the immense population of Israel ("like the sand of the sea"), only a remnant will escape the resolved destruction that God has decided. In both cases, the word carries a grave theological weight: it is the ultimate consequence of unfaithfulness or the expression of divine justice.
H3631.portee: This word reminds us that unfaithfulness to God's covenant leads to an end — not only external (military, political) but internal, to the very heart. For the believer, it invites us to take biblical warnings seriously and to seek grace rather than rebellion. Isaiah 10:22 adds a note of hope: even in the face of resolved destruction, God preserves a remnant, reminding us of His faithfulness despite judgment.

sens: Not divided, forming a complete whole
Completely consumed by fire as a sacrifice to God
Perfect, without flaw or lack
The entirety, the whole without exception
H3632.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of physical completeness: something that remains whole, without being cut or fragmented. Exodus 28:31 speaks of a robe "entirely" made of blue fabric, meaning made of a single blue cloth, without mixing in other colors.

2. In a sacrificial context, the word refers to the burnt offering, the sacrifice where the animal is completely consumed by flames — nothing is kept. 1 Samuel 7:9 shows Samuel offering a "whole" lamb as a burnt offering, which means it is completely burned, without taking a portion to eat.

3. It can also mean perfect, without defect: what is whole is complete and accomplished. Ezekiel 16:14 celebrates a beauty that is "whole," meaning perfect and finished.

4. Finally, it is used as an adverb or noun to express totality, the whole: "in whole" means completely, without anything being subtracted.
H3632.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of fullness and absence of rupture. It is related to the notion of totality and perfection. In biblical thought, what is whole pleases God; that is why sacrifices must be animals without defect, offered entirely to the Lord. The word reflects a fundamental value: integrity before God.
H3632.emploi: This word appears 15 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the books of law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and among the prophets. It is first used to qualify priestly garments and objects of worship that must be complete and without mixture (Exodus 28:31, Numbers 4:6). It also designates the burnt offering, the sacrifice completely consumed by fire (Leviticus 6:15, Deuteronomy 33:10, 1 Samuel 7:9). Among the prophets, it qualifies complete beauty or splendor (Ezekiel 16:14, 27:3, 28:12), or the total destruction of idols (Isaiah 2:18). In each context, it emphasizes the idea of totality, non-division, and fulfillment.
H3632.portee: This word invites the reader to understand the seriousness of sacrificial worship: offering something whole to God means giving without reserve, without keeping a part for oneself. It is an act of total consecration. For the Christian, it sheds light on the meaning of Christ's sacrifice, offered once for all in a complete and perfect manner. It also reminds that faith requires totality: not serving God halfway, but with all one's heart, entirely.

sens: wise man renowned in the time of Solomon
H3633G.detail: Calcol was a man recognized for his wisdom during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Kings 4:31, alongside other famous sages like Ethan, Heman, and Darda, all sons of Mahol. Solomon, the king of his time, was reputed to be wiser than all these men: "He was wiser than any man, more than Ethan the Ezrahite, more than Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol." This simple mention shows that Calcol embodied esteemed human wisdom, and that Solomon's wisdom far surpassed it.
H3633G.origine: The name Calcol means "who supports" or "who sustains" in Hebrew. He belonged to the lineage of Zerah of Judah. Like his brothers Heman and Ethan, he came from a family known for its intellectual gifts and wisdom. These men represented the pinnacle of understanding and reflection in Israel before Solomon eclipsed all the sages.
H3633G.emploi: Calcol appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:31. There he is cited among the most eminent sages of Israel, alongside Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, and Darda, all sons of Mahol. The evangelist mentions these names to establish a striking contrast: despite the great reputation of these men, Solomon was much wiser. This passage illustrates how Solomon's wisdom was exceptional and surpassed that of all the known sages of his time.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Zerah
H3633H.detail: Calcol is a man of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible as one of the five sons of Zerah. He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah in 1 Chronicles 2:6. His name is listed among those of his brothers Zimri, Ethan, Heman, and Dara. Although few details are given about him, he is known as one of the ancient sages of God's people, and biblical tradition associates him with the wise men to whom Solomon is compared. He is a representative of the descendants of Zerah in the genealogical history of Israel before the monarchy.
H3633H.origine: The name Calcol means "who sustains" or "who nourishes," derived from Hebrew roots evoking the idea of support and nourishment. This name reflects a blessing or a quality expected of the one who bears it. It is part of the naming tradition of the families of God's people, where names often carry spiritual significance or a promise.
H3633H.emploi: Calcol is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 2:6, in the genealogical list of the sons of Zerah. He belongs to the period prior to the Israelite monarchy and represents an important lineage of the tribe of Judah. Ancient tradition counts him among the wise of the people, which explains why he is cited alongside figures like Ethan and Heman, known for their wisdom. His appearance in genealogies underscores the importance of the descendants of Zerah in Israel's history.

sens: To accomplish something to its point of perfection, without anything lacking
To complete by adding what was absent or insufficient
To adorn or embellish something to make it magnificent
H3634.detail:
1. To make perfect means to bring a work or creation to its finished and flawless form. It is the idea of complete finishing: Ezekiel 27:4 describes Tyre whose builders have "made it perfect in beauty," meaning they have brought to the city all the details and qualities that make it a magnificent work.
2. To complete means to bring what is lacking so that something is whole. The workers who build a city add the essential elements until no aspect is lacking: the verb evokes this work of gradual completion.
3. To embellish and adorn fall under the same movement: in Ezekiel 27:11, the warriors decorate the walls and hang shields to "make perfect" the beauty of Tyre. The image is that of placing the final elements that make a creation shine and worthy of admiration.
H3634.origine: The root כָּלַל (kal-lal) fundamentally expresses the idea of totality and integrity. It is related to words that denote completeness and fulfillment. The verb describes the transition from incomplete to complete, from unfinished to finished: it is the action of making something whole and without lack.
H3634.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Bible, both in Ezekiel 27, a magnificent passage where the prophet depicts the splendor of Tyre before its ruin. In both occurrences (verses 4 and 11), it involves workers and warriors who complete the beauty and perfection of this great city: the builders "make it perfect" in beauty through their art, and the fighters "adorn" it with their shields and presence. The word emphasizes how a creation becomes truly admired when all its elements are in place and worked with care.
H3634.portee: This word reminds us that true beauty and true excellence do not happen by chance: they require that every detail be thought out, worked on, and completed. For the Christian, this speaks to the importance of bringing quality and care to what one undertakes, and that God Himself delights in perfecting His creations and His people to their final beauty.

sens: bring to completion, complete a construction or a work
restore what has fallen into ruin
finish building, conclude a reconstruction work
H3635A.detail:
1. Achieve means to bring an action to its conclusion, to make it complete. In Ezra 6:14, the elders of the Jews "achieve" the house of the Lord that they were rebuilding: they finish the work that was started, stone by stone, until the end.

2. The word can also mean "restore" or "rebuild" — to raise up what was brought down or ruined. In Ezra 4:12-13, it refers to "raising up" the walls of Jerusalem, that is, to reconstruct them after their destruction.

3. The context in Ezra shows that this word often carries the idea of reconstruction: it is to achieve what has been interrupted, to complete the work despite obstacles. The concrete meaning is that of a work that progresses until its final accomplishment.
H3635A.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root meaning "to complete" or "to finish." In biblical Aramaic, this verb expresses the idea of bringing something to its end or making it whole. The form used here (Shaphel and Ishtaphel) reinforces this notion of fullness and accomplishment: the action of finishing that makes the work solid and complete.
H3635A.emploi: This verb appears seven times in the book of Ezra, always in the context of the reconstruction of the Temple and the walls of Jerusalem after the exile (chapters 4, 5, and 6). It describes the stages of this great project: the adversaries of the Jews report to the king that they are "raising up" the walls, the Jews themselves explain that they are rebuilding "the house that had been built many years ago," and finally, "they achieve" the Temple. The word emphasizes both perseverance in the face of obstacles and the importance of seeing the work brought to completion.
H3635A.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer about faithfulness and perseverance in fulfilling God's will. The Jews returning from exile do not give up despite opposition: they achieve the Temple. It reminds us that our works in service to God deserve to be brought to completion, and that God blesses those who persevere until the end.

sens: An Israelite during the time of Ezra who had married a foreign woman
H3636.detail: Kelal is a man of Israel mentioned only once in the context of the return from exile. Ezra 10:30 cites him among the sons of Pachath-Moab who were to send away their foreign wives, in accordance with the decision made to restore the purity of the people returned from Babylon.
H3636.origine: The name means "completed" or "finished" in Hebrew, deriving from a root meaning "to finish" or "to accomplish." This name, borne by this man from the return from exile, may reflect the hope for restoration or fulfillment of the people after captivity.
H3636.emploi: Kelal appears only once in Ezra 10:30, in the list of descendants of Pachath-Moab who had taken foreign wives during or after the exile. This is a list drawn up by Ezra to order the dismissal of these wives, in order to preserve the religious identity of the people of Israel. This brief mention fits into the movement of separation from neighboring nations that the book of Ezra reports.

sens: Experience shame, blush with confusion, be humiliated
Be dishonored, put to confusion before others
Be insulted, outraged, offended in one's honor
Receive a mark of contempt or public dishonor
H3637.detail:
1. The word first evokes the inner feeling: one who is covered with shame experiences confusion, discomfort, and often blushes. It is the deep embarrassment of being exposed to the gaze of others. In Isaiah 50:7, the servant of the Lord declares, "I have not been dishonored": he refuses to be brought down by mockery.
2. But the word also designates the objective state: being humiliated, put in a position of inferiority or contempt. When Moses learns that his sister Miriam must remain outside the camp for seven days (Numbers 12:14), it is an act of public shame, a visible mark of dishonor.
3. The word can finally refer to the very action: to insult someone, to outrage. Job protests against his friends: "You have insulted me ten times!" (Job 19:3). It is to accuse them of inflicting contempt upon him.
H3637.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of covering with a stain or a mark: one who is covered with shame bears an invisible but real stain, which makes him inferior or suspect in the eyes of his community. In biblical Hebrew, shame is often linked to exposure (nakedness, flight, military defeat). This word can also mean to blush or to pale, as shame is visible on the face.
H3637.emploi: The word appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. It describes very diverse situations: ritual humiliation (Numbers 12:14), military defeat (2 Samuel 10:5), personal insult (Job 19:3), or the moral collapse of a nation (Jeremiah 22:22). In the Psalms, the righteous ask God that their enemies be covered with shame and that the poor do not return confused (Psalms 74:21). Isaiah uses it to express both the humiliation suffered and the prophetic refusal to suffer it (Isaiah 45:16-17). The word thus has a religious significance: true shame is that of one who turns away from God, while the righteous can count on God not to be confounded.
H3637.portee: This word helps the believer understand humiliation as a serious spiritual reality: what covers us with shame is also what separates us from God and exposes us to His judgment. But it also reveals that in the face of reproach, the righteous can stand firm in God, like the servant in Isaiah 50:7. For the reader of the Psalms, it is a prayer: asking God that our enemies sink into shame while we remain standing — it is asking for divine justice to be established.

sens: City of Assyria mentioned in ancient trade
H3638.detail: Kilmad is a city of Assyria mentioned in the prophet Ezekiel as an important commercial center. In Ezekiel 27:23, it is listed among the trading cities that trafficked with Tyre, alongside Haran, Canneh, Eden, and Sheba. Its appearance in this context of commercial prosperity suggests its role as a trading crossroads in ancient Assyria.
H3638.origine: The name Kilmad literally means "enclosure" or "enclosed place" in Assyrian, possibly evoking a fortified city or a closed place intended for commerce and exchanges. Ancient geography places it in Mesopotamia, in the trade routes of merchants between Assyria and the Mediterranean.
H3638.emploi: Kilmad appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:23. The prophet enumerates the cities that traded with Tyre at the height of its splendor. This mention fits into an oracle where Ezekiel paints a portrait of Tyre as a great trading power, before announcing its downfall. Kilmad represents a distant trading partner, attesting to the extent of the Mediterranean and Mesopotamian trade networks of the time.

sens: Public reproach, insult that affects honor
Shame, confusion, loss of dignity in the eyes of others
State of dishonor and social contempt
Humiliation suffered by one who has committed a fault
H3639.detail:
1. Opprobrium is primarily a word: a reproach publicly addressed to someone to mock or offend them. It is the insult that wounds honor. In Job 20:3, the speaker says he has heard reproaches that outrage him, words that offend him.
2. It is also the shame felt: the confusion, the feeling of being dishonored in the eyes of others. In Psalms 69:8, the psalmist speaks of shame that covers his face — he blushes, he is publicly humiliated.
3. Opprobrium designates the state of dishonor itself: the condition of one who is despised. In Ezekiel 16:52, Jerusalem must bear its opprobrium, meaning to live in contempt and dishonor because of its sins.
4. Finally, it is the humiliation suffered as a consequence of a fault. In Proverbs 18:13, one who answers without listening brings confusion upon themselves — they cover themselves with shame through their folly.
H3639.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to lack," "to be deprived of." Opprobrium is therefore what one is deprived of: dignity, honor, respect. This is why the term designates both the insult received and the resulting shame. The central idea is one of loss: one loses face, one loses reputation, one is brought low.
H3639.emploi: This word appears 29 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in the Psalms, in Isaiah, and in Ezekiel. It is especially mentioned when the Bible speaks of the consequences of sin or injustice. The faithful ask God to deliver them from the opprobrium inflicted by their enemies (Psalms 35:26, 44:16). The prophets warn that opprobrium follows disobedience: Jerusalem bears its opprobrium (Ezekiel 16:52) or the wicked nations bear it unto death (Ezekiel 32:25). But the Bible also promises that God will remove the opprobrium: Isaiah 61:7 announces that instead of disgrace, the redeemed will have a double portion and everlasting joy.
H3639.portee: This word reminds the believer that sin has real social and spiritual consequences: it dishonors us, exposes us to shame and contempt. But it also teaches us that God can remove this opprobrium. For those who suffer unjust shame, there is comfort in the Psalms: those who bear opprobrium for following God can count on His deliverance and restoration. It is a word against shame and for the dignity restored in Christ.

sens: State of one who has lost their honor, who has committed an unworthy act
Public contempt, dishonor that attaches to a person or a people
H3640.detail:
1. Shame is the painful state of one who has lost their honor or dignity in the eyes of others. It is the sensation of deep humiliation that results from reprehensible conduct or defeat. In Jeremiah 23:40, God announces that He will place upon the false prophets an "everlasting shame": they will bear forever the mark of their unworthiness, unable to erase or forget it.
2. Shame also designates the public dishonor itself, the lasting contempt that a community attaches to someone or an entire people. It is the opposite of glory and honor, and it can persist from generation to generation if it remains engraved in collective memory.
H3640.origine: The Hebrew word derives from a root that expresses the idea of mockery, derision. Shame is not simply an inner emotion: it is a public, visible state, of which one is the object before others. This root belongs to a family of words that all express humiliation and social contempt.
H3640.emploi: This word appears only once in the biblical text in Hebrew. It is found in the prophecy of Jeremiah addressed to the false prophets: God promises to strike them with an "everlasting shame" that will become proverbial and memorable. The context shows that shame here is a consequence of divine judgment, a lasting sanction attached to lies and unfaithfulness to God. It is a punishment that transcends the life of the guilty and is inscribed in the memory of generations.
H3640.portee: Biblical shame is not a mere emotion: it is the expression of God's judgment on sin, particularly on those who deceive in the name of God. For the believer, this word reminds us that public missteps and unfaithfulness lead to lasting, visible consequences that mark memory. It thus calls for sincerity and faithfulness in our words and actions.

sens: Ancient Babylonian city mentioned among the cities founded by Nimrod
H3641A.detail: Calneh is a city of Babylon mentioned in Genesis as one of the main cities of Nimrod's kingdom, alongside Babel, Erech, and Accad, all located in the land of Shinar (ancient Mesopotamia). It is a historical site of early Mesopotamian civilization, the capital of a pre-flood empire (Genesis 10:10).
H3641A.origine: The name "Calneh" (or "Calno" in other biblical texts) means "fortress of Anu" in Akkadian, where Anu is the god of heaven in Mesopotamian mythology. It designates an ancient city of Babylon, possibly identified with Niffer or Nippur. This name appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogical list of Noah's sons that establishes the peoples and cities of the post-flood era.
H3641A.emploi: Calneh appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 10:10, where it is listed among the four great cities of Nimrod's reign in Shinar. This biblical passage enumerates the foundations of the first human empire after the flood, marking the expansion and political organization of the descendants of Ham. The context situates Calneh as a major urban center of early Babylonian civilization, reflecting the power and ambition of ancient Mesopotamian kingdoms.

sens: Ancient Assyrian city located near Aleppo
H3641B.detail: Calneh is an important city of the ancient world, located in Assyria near Aleppo, in present-day northern Syria. It was conquered by Assyria in the 8th century B.C. The prophet Amos mentions it in a rebuke addressed to the proud Israelites: he invites them to "pass to Calneh" and see that even such prestigious and prosperous cities have succumbed to Assyrian power (Amos 6:2). Isaiah refers to it in a similar context, reminding that the king of Assyria boasted of having taken this city, as if it were proof of his invincibility (Isaiah 10:9).
H3641B.origine: The name "Calneh" comes from an Assyrian root and would mean "fortress of Anu" (Anu being an Assyrian deity). It was one of the great cities of the Assyrian empire.
H3641B.emploi: Calneh appears twice in the Old Testament, both in prophetic messages from the 8th century B.C. Amos uses it to humiliate the pride of the northern and southern kingdoms of Israel by comparing them to this great conquered city. Isaiah mentions it as an example of the vain pride of the king of Assyria, who boasted of his military victories without recognizing that it is God who controls history. These two prophets cite Calneh for the same reason: to show that human power, however imposing, is fragile and subject to God's judgment.

sens: To intensely yearn for something or someone, with a kind of painful desire
To experience a visceral, physical lack, like a thirst of the whole body
To ardently seek a lost or distant presence or relationship
H3642.detail:
1. The verb הָמַה (kamah) expresses a desire that stirs the whole being: it is not a simple wish, but a deep aspiration that exhausts the one who feels it. The image is that of a soul that weakens, slowly fading away due to lack — hence the literal translation 'to weaken' or 'to fade away from desire.' In Psalms 63:2, the psalmist says that his body 'longs' for God, as if he is melting away, drying up in the desert far from the one he seeks.
2. This verb paints a desire that is both physical and spiritual: it is the whole body that languishes, not just the spirit. The psalmist compares his state to that of a dry land without water — an image of drought, of physical decay caused by absence.
3. Kamah is less the expression of a polite request than the cry of an inner urgency: the one who longs for something needs it to live, just as the desert needs rain. It is the language of one who has tasted a presence or joy and can no longer do without it.
H3642.origine: The root כָּמַה (kamah) literally means 'to dry up,' 'to fade away.' It evokes the image of a creature losing its strength, withering away — the ardent desire being perceived as a form of exhaustion, a premature aging of the one who languishes. The word carries the idea that the lack of what one loves consumes, weakens, empties of life.
H3642.emploi: The verb kamah appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 63:2, where it describes the psalmist's desire for God. It is a word of extreme intimacy: the poet is not ashamed to admit that his physical body, and not just his spirit, thirsts for the presence of his God. The context is one of separation — the psalmist is in a desert land, separated from the temple and the house of God — and his whole body longs, as if he is perishing, towards the one he loves.
H3642.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to consider that the desire for God should not be shameful or intellectual, but physical and visceral: prayer, the search for His presence, is an act that engages the whole being, body and soul. It reminds us that faith is not primarily a doctrine, but a relationship of love that affects our entire existence. The one who 'longs for' God acknowledges his absolute necessity, just as the hungry need bread.

sens: Son or companion of Barzillai the Gileadite
The one who followed King David across the Jordan
The inn in Bethlehem founded on his possession
H3643.detail:
1. Kimham is a young man who accompanies Barzillai, an elderly and wealthy man from Gilead, when he escorts King David after his flight during Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 19:37). Barzillai asks the king to take care of Kimham since he himself is too old to continue; he is likely his son or a close relative.
2. King David agrees to let Kimham follow him and promises to do good to him, accepting whatever Kimham wishes (2 Samuel 19:38). Kimham therefore crosses the Jordan with David and becomes one of his royal protégés.
3. David gives Kimham a possession in Bethlehem, his hometown; on this land, an inn is established that bears his name in subsequent generations, thus creating a lasting legacy of this act of royal kindness.
H3643.origine: The name Kimham means 'their desire' or 'their aspiration,' composed of a Hebrew word evoking ardent desire. It is a typical name from the ancient Semitic world, reflecting a quality or aspiration at the time of his birth. The character and the place of the same name enter the historical memory of Israel as symbols of King David's generosity towards a deserving young man.
H3643.emploi: Kimham appears three times in 2 Samuel 19:37-40, all verses concerning the same event: the crossing of the Jordan with David. Barzillai first requests the king to take Kimham under his protection, the king agrees and promises his favor, then Kimham actually accompanies the king and all the people. The usages show the importance of this diplomatic moment: the king seals his alliance with the people of Gilead by agreeing to take care of the young man. Subsequently, an inn bears his name in Bethlehem, proof that David kept his promise by giving him a possession.
H3643.portee: The story of Kimham illustrates the value that David places on loyalty and courage. It shows how an act of royal kindness towards a young man can be remembered and bear fruit for generations — the inn of Kimham becomes a landmark in Bethlehem. It is also an example of the king's gratitude towards those who supported him in adversity, a virtue that God's people are called to imitate.

sens: in the same way as, according to the manner in which
like, similar to, resembling
at the moment when, when
so to speak, in a sense
H3644G.detail: 1. This word expresses a comparison of manner: it indicates that two things are done or occur in the same way, the same manner. Example: 'Get up, take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you perish in the destruction of the city' (Genesis 19:15) — the action unfolds according to the described urgency. 2. It marks a resemblance between two beings or two things: one is like the other. Example: 'What man has ever heard, as we have, the voice of the living God?' (Deuteronomy 5:26) — no one has had a similar experience. 'Before Josiah, there was no king who, like him, returned to the Lord' (2 Kings 23:25) — no other king resembled him in his conversion. 3. It indicates the moment, the point in time at which something occurs, often rendered by 'when' or 'as.' This is a temporal nuance of the same word. 4. It softens an assertion, introducing a mitigated or approximate comparison: 'the earth transforms as clay that receives an imprint' (Job 38:14) — it is an image, a metaphorical comparison.
H3644G.origine: This word comes from ancient Hebrew roots that evoke equality and resemblance. Originally, it combines the idea of 'as' and 'according to,' expressing both analogy and conformity. The word belongs to a broad family denoting equivalence, parity. It is very common in biblical Hebrew to introduce comparisons that fill poetry and narrative prose.
H3644G.emploi: This word is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible (126 occurrences noted), present in all books, from historical narratives to psalms and wisdom texts. In narratives (Genesis, Exodus, Samuel, Kings), it serves to compare beings: thus it is said that a man is 'as' another, that a king has no equal. In the poetry of the Psalms, it introduces images of God: 'Who is like You, powerful Lord?' (Psalms 89:9). In descriptions (Job), it enumerates resemblances: 'the earth will be torn to pieces like a garment, and its inhabitants will perish like flies' (Isaiah 51:6). Its meaning nuances according to context: strict quality comparison (Deuteronomy 5:26), conformity to a model (Deuteronomy 18:15), implicit temporal condition (Genesis 19:15).
H3644G.portee: This word teaches us that the Bible thinks in images and resemblances. By reading how it compares God, beings, events, we learn to see spiritual realities through their visible reflections. The great biblical affirmations about the uniqueness of God ('Who is like the Lord?') gain strength through this comparative structure: it invites us to recognize that nothing equals divine power and faithfulness. This humble word reminds us that biblical faith is expressed through concrete images, comparisons drawn from everyday life.

sens: Place of refuge near Bethlehem
H3644H.detail: Kimham is a place mentioned only once in the Bible, designated as an inn or resting place located near Bethlehem. It is where the survivors of the massacre of Gedaliah stopped before retreating to Egypt (Jeremiah 41:17). The name evokes a refuge where travelers could find hospitality and shelter.
H3644H.origine: The name Kimham is composed of two elements: it combines Geruth ("Geruth", a term that refers to a dwelling or lodging) with a prefix or suffix that forms the proper name. This place likely bears the name of a man who ran an inn or of a former owner who became famous for his hospitality.
H3644H.emploi: Kimham appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 41:17. It is mentioned as the gathering point where the survivors of Gedaliah's murder regrouped before fleeing to Egypt, fearing retaliation from the Babylonians. This place thus holds historical and political significance in the final days of the kingdom of Judah.

sens: National deity of the Moabites and god of the Ammonites
H3645.detail: Chemosh is the name of the god that the Moabites worshiped as their protective and national deity. The Ammonites also revered him. This god appears in the Old Testament as a foreign power to which neighboring peoples turned for protection and prosperity, as indicated by the appeal of the king of Judah to Jephthah: "What your god Chemosh gives you to possess, will you not possess it?" (Judges 11:24). Unfortunately, this worship penetrated even to Jerusalem when Solomon built a high place in his honor (1 Kings 11:7), which the Bible designates as an abomination. Only the intervention of King Josiah allowed for the demolition of these idolatrous sanctuaries (2 Kings 23:13). The worship of Chemosh symbolizes in the biblical text the unfaithfulness to God and the abandonment of the ways of the Lord.
H3645.origine: The name Chemosh literally means "the subjugator" or "the one who subdues." His worship was deeply rooted in ancient Moabite religion, evidenced by historical inscriptions. Biblical texts sometimes associate him with other pagan gods (Baal-Peor, Baal-Zebub) to denote various manifestations of idolatrous worship. He is a god of Canaanite and Moabite mythology, radically opposed to the one true God of Israel.
H3645.emploi: Chemosh appears eight times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the historical and prophetic books (Numbers, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Jeremiah). He is systematically presented as the object of culpable idolatry: first, the cry of pain from the Moabites in the face of their defeat (Numbers 21:29), then the miserable trust they place in him (Judges 11:24). The introduction of his worship in Jerusalem under Solomon marks a turning point in Israel's spiritual drama (1 Kings 11:7, 11:33), and his destruction by Josiah is the necessary correction (2 Kings 23:13). The prophet Jeremiah announces that Chemosh himself will be taken captive (Jeremiah 48:7), illustrating the ultimate powerlessness of false gods in the face of the Lord's judgment.
H3645.portee: The account of Chemosh teaches the Christian reader the reality of the trap of idolatry: even a faithful king like Solomon, when he abandons the living God, leads the nation toward spiritual ruin. This historical example shows that trust in false gods—whether ancient or modern—can only bring captivity and defeat. Conversely, it highlights the importance of remaining attached to the one true God and rejecting anything that usurps His place in our hearts.

sens: Small aromatic seed used as a spice or condiment
Plant sown and harvested in the ancient Near East
H3646.detail:
1. Cumin is a small aromatic seed, light brown in color, used as a spice to enhance dishes. In Isaiah 28:25, the prophet mentions the sower who "spreads dill and sows cumin" among various crops: it is a common agricultural product, cultivated alongside wheat and barley in the fields of the Near East.
2. It is a plant that is harvested delicately: unlike dill, which is trampled with a sledge, cumin cannot withstand this harsh treatment (Isaiah 28:27). Instead, "cumin is beaten with a rod," meaning it is lightly struck to detach the small seeds without crushing or losing them. The prophet uses this example to show that God, in His chastisements, adapts His strength to each people: He acts with the wisdom of a farmer who adjusts his actions to the grain he is handling.
H3646.origine: The Hebrew word kammon derives from a root that expresses the idea of fineness and smallness (cumin seeds are tiny). It is the name of a well-known plant in Egypt and the Levant, cultivated since antiquity as a spice. In Greek, this word became "kyminon," and the Romans called it "cuminum."
H3646.emploi: Cumin appears twice in the Bible, both in Isaiah 28, verses 25 and 27. The context is instructive: the prophet Isaiah uses the image of the farmer who wisely sows his field to teach Israel that God acts with intelligence and restraint towards His people. Cumin serves as a concrete example of a seed that requires delicate handling during harvest, unlike other hardier grains. It is a simply agricultural and concrete word, without particular spiritual charge: Isaiah chooses it precisely because his readers were familiar with it from daily life.
H3646.portee: This passage teaches us that God always acts with wisdom suited to the situation. Just as the farmer does not treat cumin like barley, God does not administer the same judgment to each people, but adjusts His actions to what He knows is just for each. It is an image of divine providence: God knows the grain He cultivates and knows how to harvest it.

sens: to put away, keep secret
to preserve carefully, put away safely
H3647.detail:
1. To hide primarily means to put something away, to keep it secretly, like storing a treasure that one does not want to see scattered. In Deuteronomy 32:34, the Lord speaks of anger that He has "hidden," kept in reserve near Him, sealed in His treasures—meaning that He retains it, reserving it for the day of judgment.
2. By extension, to hide means to preserve carefully, to put away to protect. It is the idea of setting aside something precious or serious, like sealing an important letter in a chest.
H3647.origine: The verb כָּמַס (kamas) comes from a Hebrew root that denotes the action of accumulating or setting aside. It is a rare verb in the Old Testament, evoking the concrete image of a treasure that is closed, sealed, kept out of sight. The root suggests vigilant preservation, an intentional setting aside.
H3647.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 32:34. It is used in the context of the Song of Moses, where God affirms that His anger and judgment are "hidden," meaning retained and kept in reserve until the time of punishment. It is a solemn word, emphasizing the certainty and gravity of the divine judgment that will come.
H3647.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment is never forgotten or annulled, even if it seems delayed. It invites us to take divine justice seriously and to understand that God "keeps" His verdict in reserve with the same certainty as one seals a treasure securely. It is a grave word for one who turns away from God.

sens: To experience an inner warmth that stirs the heart and bowels
To feel deep compassion, a tenderness that manifests physically
To be burning, heated to white
To be deeply troubled by an emotion
H3648.detail:
1. The word first describes a physical reaction: an inner warmth that rises in the body and stirs it. In Genesis 43:30, Joseph is seized by such a strong emotion for his brother Benjamin that his bowels are "moved" — he must leave the room quickly to weep. It is as if an inner flame is burning in his heart.
2. This warmth is inseparable from compassion and tenderness. In 1 Kings 3:26, the true mother feels her bowels "move" for her son when she learns that he is to be killed: her maternal love burns in her heart and compels her to plead with the king. The emotion here is the expression of bond and affection.
3. The word can also describe a physical, literal burning: in Lamentations 5:10, during the famine, the skin of the people is "burning like an oven" from the "fervor" of hunger — a heat of suffering that consumes the body.
4. Finally, it is to be deeply agitated within. In Hosea 11:8, God says that his heart "is stirred" within him when he thinks of delivering Israel: his compassions are "moved." It is the emotion of a heart divided between justice and mercy.
H3648.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes heat, combustion, warming. The starting image is physical: something that heats, that burns. In Hebrew, the bowels (the heart, the intestines) are the seat of intense emotions. When they are "heated" or "moved," it means a passion is stirring within — tenderness, pity, or suffering. The Greek translates this with the verb meaning "to stir" or "to be moved."
H3648.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the Niphal form (passive or reflexive). It is used to describe strong emotions, often related to familial love or compassion. In Genesis 43:30 and 1 Kings 3:26, it denotes the emotion of a loving heart that cannot contain its tenderness. In Hosea 11:8, it expresses God's own inner turmoil — his compassions trembling when he contemplates the punishment of his people. In Lamentations 5:10, the same word describes a burning of suffering. In all cases, it is an emotion that does not remain merely mental: it moves the bowels and the body.
H3648.portee: This word shows us that true emotions — especially tenderness and compassion — are not weak sentimentalities, but forces that shake our entire being. When God says that his compassions are "moved," he reveals that his heart is alive, not indifferent. For the reader, it is an invitation not to despise our legitimate emotions of pity or love: they come from the heart, just as warmth comes from fire.

sens: One who officiates in the worship of false gods, idols, or pagan deities
The minister of a religion foreign to the God of Israel, responsible for sacrifices and offerings
H3649.detail:
1. It is a man dedicated to the service of idols and false gods. He performs for these non-gods the functions that a true priest performs for the living God: he offers sacrifices, burns incense, and celebrates rites. In 2 Kings 23:5, King Josiah "removed the priests of the idols" who, in the high places of Judah, burned incense to Baal, the sun, and the moon — they were the official ministers of these false cults.
2. This word also designates, by extension, one who serves an idol or a false god, even if his role is not always that of a priest in the strict sense. In Hosea 10:5, during the fall of Samaria, "its priests will tremble for it," meaning for the idol of the golden calves: these are the servants of this impious cult who see what they served collapse.
H3649.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "shaman" or "magician," one who practices occult or superstitious rites. It designates less a priest according to the legitimate order than someone who dedicates himself to deviant religious practices, without true authority, counterfeiting the role of true priesthood. The term marks a clear distinction: a true priest (kohen) serves the God of Israel; a komer serves lies.
H3649.emploi: This word appears three times in the Old Testament, always in a context of denouncing idolatrous worship or its destruction. In 2 Kings 23:5, King Josiah "removes" them during his religious reform to purify Judah. In Hosea 10:5, they "tremble" in fear when the idol they served is about to disappear. In Zephaniah 1:4, the Lord "destroys" them along with the remnants of Baal. The emphasis is always on their illegitimacy and the end of their function: they are not true priests, and their worship is doomed to destruction.
H3649.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible makes a radical distinction between the true worship of the true God and religious counterfeits. It does not treat false gods and their servants with indifference: it denounces them. For the believer, it is an exhortation to vigilance: idolatry can wear the garments of true worship, with its priests and rites, but it remains a seduction of lies. Only the worship of the living God, according to his revelation, is true.

sens: The obscurity, the absence of light
The black hue, the dark color
Figuratively, what is gloomy, threatening, distressing
H3650.detail:
1. Darkness primarily denotes deep obscurity, the absence of daylight. In Job 3:5, it is a darkness that seizes the day of Job's birth, enveloping it like a threatening shadow.
2. The word can also refer to the color black itself, the dark hue of things.
3. Figuratively and spiritually, darkness evokes what is threatening, sinister, filled with anguish and terror — everything that terrifies the soul in moments of distress, as in Job who curses the day of his birth.
H3650.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root קמר (kamar), which expresses the idea of darkening, becoming black. It belongs to the family of Hebrew words describing dark hues and obscurity, particularly what is thick, dense, impenetrable — like the darkness of a moonless night or the gloomy atmosphere of a storm.
H3650.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 3:5. It is used by Job in his final discourse, where he curses the day of his birth, imploring darkness to seize it. The darkness here is not a mere absence of light: it is a dark and oppressive power that represents the misfortune, desolation, and dread that overwhelm Job in his extreme suffering.
H3650.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, darkness is often the image of what distances us from God, of distress and misfortune. For the Christian reader, this underscores how precious and salvific divine light is, and how faith can traverse the darkest moments of life.

sens: Conforming to truth, honest, trustworthy
Just, correct, well-founded
Appropriate, suitable, fitting well
H3651A.detail:
1. Sincere: that which is true, honest, without deception. In Genesis 42:11 and 42:31, Joseph's brothers repeat "we are sincere" to assert that they are not spies, that they are telling the truth about who they are. It is the integrity of word and heart.
2. Just and correct: that which is upright, legal, in accordance with good order. In 2 Kings 17:9, Israel does "things that are not right," meaning contrary to righteousness and the will of God.
3. Appropriate, fitting: that which is relevant or judicious in a situation. In Proverbs 15:7, "the heart of the wise proclaims righteousness" — meaning that the wise speak wisely, with discernment. The idea is that speech or action fits well with the circumstance.
H3651A.origine: The Hebrew word ken comes from a root that denotes the idea of establishing, fixing, making stable. From this comes the meaning of what is "firm," "solid," "true" — that on which one can rely. The word is also related to the adjective "upright": what is truly upright is reliable and honest. This root appears in other Hebrew words to express solidity and truth.
H3651A.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the provided biblical usages, mainly in the Old Testament. Its most frequent use concerns honesty and sincerity: in Genesis 42, Joseph's brothers use it to justify themselves before the Egyptian governor and assert that they are not spies. It is also found to describe what is just or correct: in 2 Kings 17:9 for acts that are not fitting, in Proverbs for wisdom and justice. The word can also qualify what is appropriate or relevant in speech and action. Its meaning varies slightly depending on the context: sometimes it emphasizes factual truth, sometimes conformity to what is just or right.
H3651A.portee: This word reminds the believer of the importance of sincerity and integrity: being "sincere" is not just about not lying, it is about living in accordance with truth, with what is just and right. It is also about doing things properly, wisely, and thoughtfully. For the Bible reader, ken invites one to seek truth, to flee from lies and deception, and to align one's life with God's justice.

sens: Introduces a reason, a cause, or a motive
Expresses acceptance of a given reality or situation
Marks a conclusion that follows from an established reason
H3651B.detail:
1. The word introduces the reason why something is true, occurs, or must be done. It is the cause or motive for an action: in Genesis 38:26, Judah says to Tamar, "She is less guilty than I, since I did not give her to Shelah, my son" — he explains why she deserves more compassion than he does, recalling what he failed to do.
2. The word also serves to acknowledge a state of fact that one accepts as a starting point: in Numbers 10:31, Moses says to Hobab, "since you know the places where we camp in the wilderness" — he starts from the acknowledgment that Hobab has this knowledge to ask him to stay as a guide.
3. Sometimes it marks a transition or a judgment that logically follows from what has just been said, sealing a reason in a decision: in 2 Samuel 18:20, Joab denies the messenger the honor of bringing the news "since the king's son is dead" — this death is the reason that changes the status of the news.
H3651B.origine: The Hebrew word "ken" literally means "thus" or "therefore," expressing a consequence or an established state. When preceded by "ki" ("for," "that"), it forms a conjunctive phrase "ki al ken" or "ki ken" that strengthens the causality: "for it is thus that," "since this is the case." This construction is based on the idea of a reality posed as a foundation.
H3651B.emploi: This word appears ten times in the provided usages, especially in historical and prophetic books. In Genesis and Numbers, it justifies requests or refusals: "since you know the places" (Numbers 10:31), "since I did not give her" (Genesis 38:26). In 2 Samuel 18:20, it motivates an immediate decision. In Jeremiah, it can also express a bitter acknowledgment: "since you know" becomes "it (captivity) will be long" (Jeremiah 29:28), and in Jeremiah 38:4, the translation "discourages" shows that the context emphasizes the practical consequence: this man discourages because he holds such discourse. The word remains fundamentally causal, although its rhetorical effect varies according to the speaker's tone.
H3651B.portee: This small word reminds us that in Scripture, actions and words are motivated by solid realities. It invites us to seek the true reasons behind the decisions or commandments we encounter, and to accept them not as arbitrary orders, but as wise responses to an established situation. It is a call to logical coherence in faith.

sens: In this manner, in this way
Therefore, thus
Equally, likewise
Exactly, precisely
And then, afterwards
Since, so that
H3651C.detail:
1. The word designates the manner in which something is done or occurs: it refers to the concrete way just described. In Genesis 1:7, after God created the expanse, the text says "and it was so," meaning that the action took place exactly as stated. In Numbers 12:7, God says of Moses, "not so with my servant," meaning that Moses does not behave like other prophets.
2. The word marks the consequence or reason for an act: it introduces a logical conclusion. In Psalms 45:3, "therefore God has blessed you" explains that beauty and grace lead to divine blessing. In Ezekiel 11:16, "therefore you shall say" announces judgment in reaction to the described situation.
3. The word creates a comparison or equality: it shows that two things operate in the same way. In 2 Samuel 20:18, the woman explains that matters were "resolved thus," meaning through consultation and wisdom, as was the ancient custom.
4. The word reinforces or confirms the accuracy of a previous action or state.
5. The word can mark a temporal or logical sequence.
6. The word serves as a connector in conditional or causal statements.
H3651C.origine: The Hebrew word ken comes from a very ancient root meaning establishment or fixity. It is a demonstrative adverb: it points to a manner of doing or a situation, as if saying "here is how" or "in this way." In biblical Hebrew, this very frequent small word becomes one of the major logical connectors of the text, serving to weave the narrative and mark transitions between actions and consequences.
H3651C.emploi: This word is one of the most common in the Hebrew Bible, with 708 occurrences. It appears from the beginning of Genesis to the last prophets, serving as a backbone to the narrative and argumentative text. In the creation narrative (Genesis 1), it punctuates each day — "and it was so" — marking the fulfillment of God's word. In laws and instructions, it introduces consequences or concrete applications. Among the prophets, it becomes the rhetorical tool par excellence to transition from diagnosis to judgment or from promise to fulfillment. Its meaning varies according to context: sometimes it is purely descriptive ("the thing was done thus"), sometimes it is logical ("therefore"), sometimes it is temporal ("then"), but it always connects elements of discourse.
H3651C.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God acts with order and coherence: when Scripture says "thus," it affirms that what happens corresponds to God's plan and word. It is a word of certainty: what is said is done, according to the stated manner. It is also a word of moral causality: actions have consequences, promises are fulfilled, judgment follows iniquity. Meditating on this small word helps to see the Bible not as a collection of stories, but as a narrative where everything holds together and where God masters the sequences.

sens: in this manner, in this way
introducing what will be said or reported
confirming or concluding a previous statement
H3652.detail:
1. The word marks a manner of acting or being: something is done or has been done "thus," that is, in such a way. In Ezra 5:3, the governors come to speak "thus" to the builders, meaning they address them with a specific question.
2. It introduces the direct speech that follows: what comes next specifies the content of what has been said. In Daniel 2:24, Daniel says to Arioch "thus" — the following phrase reports his own words: "Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon."
3. It can reinforce or conclude a statement, marking assurance or conviction. The word gives the discourse a declarative force, as if the speaker is saying: "This is how things happened or will happen."
H3652.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to stand, to be stable, to be established." The initial image is that of fixity: something that stands firm. That is why "ken" also carries an affirmative sense — what is established and certain. In Aramaic, the word retains this same sense of "thus, in this manner," with a nuance of affirmation and certainty. The Hebrew variant is related to verbs expressing stability and confirmation.
H3652.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Bible, exclusively in the Aramaic portions of Ezra and Daniel. It regularly serves as an introducer of direct speech: instead of simply saying "he spoke," the author says "he spoke thus," and then reports the exact words (Ezra 5:3; Daniel 2:24-25; Daniel 4:14; Daniel 6:6). It can also accompany the narration to indicate how an action is accomplished. This repetition emphasizes the importance of the reported speech and gives the text a solemn and precise character, typical of the administrative and narrative style of Ezra and Daniel.
H3652.portee: For the reader, this small word is a signal: it announces that the words that will follow are decisive for the story. By reading "thus," one knows that they will hear the voice of a central character — a king, a sage, an official — and that these words are reported faithfully. It is a call to attention, inviting the believer to listen with the same seriousness as the actors in the narrative.

sens: Base or physical support on which an object rests
Foundation or foot of a structure
Function, position, or charge that someone occupies
Condition or social status of a person
H3653.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the material support of an object — the base or pedestal on which it rests. In Israelite worship, the bronze basin intended for the priests' ablutions was provided with a bronze base that kept it stable (Exodus 30:18). It is the same word for the legs or feet of the temple furniture: the vertical structures that support the whole (1 Kings 7:29).
2. By extension, the word can refer to the foundation or base of a construction, that is, what makes it solid and durable.
3. Figuratively, a "base" becomes a social position: the charge or function that someone occupies in the established order. The chief of the cupbearers of Pharaoh implores Joseph to help him regain "his position," that is, his post with the king (Genesis 40:13).
4. More broadly, it can refer to the state or condition of a person in the hierarchy — their place in society. In the prophet Daniel, the word is used to describe the establishment of a king on his throne or dominion (Daniel 11:7, 11:20).
H3653.origine: The Hebrew word kèn comes from a root meaning "to set up, to establish, to place upright." It evokes the idea of placing something solidly in a vertical position. It is found in other Hebrew words designating what is durable or established. The image is very material: before being used in the figurative sense of "function" or "condition," the word first depicts the act of erecting or founding.
H3653.emploi: This word appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is particularly frequent in the description of worship: the base of the washing basin appears several times (Exodus 30:18, 30:28, 31:9, 38:8, 40:11, Leviticus 8:11), as it is an important detail of the sanctuary's equipment. The word is also used for the structures of Solomon's temple, notably the legs or feet of the altar (1 Kings 7:29-31). In a more abstract and political sense, it designates the charge or position of a servant of the king (Genesis 40:13, 41:13) and, in the prophet Daniel, the establishment of a king on his throne (Daniel 11:7, 11:20, 11:21, 11:38). The word thus shifts from the concrete to the figurative while retaining the idea of stability and establishment.
H3653.portee: This word reminds us that stability — whether of a material construction or a social position — rests on a solid base. In biblical worship, the washing basin with its base evokes the necessity of a reliable structure to properly carry out the service of God. On a personal level, it invites reflection on what underpins our lives: on what bases do we establish our responsibilities and our place in the world?

sens: Small harmful insect that attacks skin and clothing
Insignificant, fragile creature destined for destruction
H3654.detail:
1. The louse is a tiny parasitic insect. In Exodus 8:12-14, during the plagues of Egypt, the dust of the ground turns into lice that cover men and beasts: it is a massive and humiliating calamity, which even the Egyptian magicians cannot imitate. The text emphasizes the impotence of the magicians in the face of this divine plague.
2. By extension, the louse symbolizes the fragility and insignificance of what perishes. In Isaiah 51:6, the inhabitants of the earth "will perish like flies" (or "like lice") — an image of their smallness before the eternity of God. In Psalms 105:31, it is also associated with the other plagues, as proof of the Lord's power over nature.
H3654.origine: The Hebrew word kèn primarily denotes the louse or head louse (Pediculus humanus). It is a real and observable animal, hated in antiquity as a parasite. The Bible also uses it as an image of weakness: that which is small, fragile, mortal. The word appears mainly in the accounts of the plagues of Egypt, where it embodies God's judgment on creatures — even the most insignificant — over which He has free reign.
H3654.emploi: The word kèn appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. Four times in Exodus 8 (the third plague), where the dust of Egypt turns into lice: it is a remarkable punishment, as no ancient insecticide could stop it. Once in Psalms 105:31, which summarizes the plagues by celebrating the Lord's victory. Once in Isaiah 51:6, where the louse is a poetic image of human mortality. The word remains rare in Scripture: it serves to strike the reader's imagination by its very strangeness.
H3654.portee: The louse reminds the reader that God sovereignly disposes of every creature, even the most despised or invisible. It is a lesson in humility: the powerful of Egypt, powerless against parasites, discover that their dominion is nothing before the word of the Lord. For the believer, this encourages trust: the God who reigns over lice reigns over all obstacles that seem insurmountable to me.

sens: To give someone a nickname, to call them by a flattering title or epithet
To use words of complacency or excessive praise to please
To pronounce a name with tenderness or affection
H3655.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the action of giving someone a title, a nickname, or an honorific term — often a title that exaggerates their qualities or merits to please them. It is a way of honoring them by calling them by a name that flatters.
2. By extension, it means to flatter someone in the sense we understand: to address them with pleasant or excessive words to please them, to seduce them, or to obtain something from them. Elihu clearly states: "I do not know how to flatter" (Job 32:22), meaning he refuses this deceptive complacency.
3. More gently, the word can also refer to the act of pronouncing a name with tenderness or love — as in Isaiah 44:5, where one "will pronounce the name of Israel with love," suggesting sincere affection rather than deception.
H3655.origine: The Hebrew root knh originally evokes the idea of naming, calling, giving a title. It is related to the notion of designation, of naming. The verb in its intensive form (Piel) emphasizes this action: to give a special title, a nickname, particularly a flattering title. The image is that of the word that creates or redefines someone's identity through a chosen name.
H3655.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, all in serious contexts where the question of the sincerity of words arises. Job 32:21-22 uses it in the negative sense of dangerous flattery: Elihu swears that he will flatter no one in judging Job's words, for that would displease God. In Isaiah 44:5 and 45:4, the term takes on a more positive hue: it is no longer about deceptive complacency, but about the tenderness with which one pronounces the name of Jacob or Israel, or the love with which God calls Cyrus by name. Thus, the word oscillates between suspect deception and sincere affection.
H3655.portee: This word highlights the power of words — they can flatter and deceive, or they can affirm an identity with tenderness and truth. For the believer, it serves as a reminder that flattery is a trap, a form of dishonesty toward God and others, while speaking to someone with genuine affection and respect honors their dignity.

sens: Ancient city of Mesopotamia, important commercial center
H3656.detail: Cannae is a city mentioned in the Bible as a prosperous trading center in ancient Mesopotamia. It was among the trading partners of Tyre, the great Phoenician trading power. In Ezekiel 27:23, the prophet lists the cities that "traded" with Tyre: Cannae is cited alongside Haran and Eden, showing its importance in the trade networks of the time. This mention in a funeral hymn addressed to Tyre underscores the wealth and commercial influence of these cities.
H3656.origine: The name "Cannae" comes from the Hebrew כַּנֶּה (kan.neh), which etymologically means "to give a flattering title" or "to honor." It is a proper name that designates a city in the region of Mesopotamia. In the Greek Septuagint (translation of the Old Testament), it is sometimes identified with Calneh (כַּלְנֵה, kal.neh), another ancient city in the region.
H3656.emploi: Cannae appears only once in the Bible: in Ezekiel 27:23. The prophet Ezekiel, at the time of Tyre's fall, lists the peoples and cities that had commercial relations with this Phoenician metropolis. Cannae is mentioned as one of these trading cities, alongside Haran (in northern Mesopotamia) and Eden (a fertile region). This historical reference illustrates the vast trade networks of ancient Near Eastern antiquity and places Cannae among the prosperous cities of Mesopotamia.

sens: To keep safe, to defend against danger or destruction
To support, to keep upright (as a root or support holds up a tree)
H3657.detail:
1. To keep safe, to defend against danger or destruction. The psalmist asks God to protect what His right hand has planted — an image to designate the people of Israel that God has established. It is an active protection, one that preserves from ruin (Psalms 80:16).
2. To support, to keep upright. This sense comes from the image of a root or a stem that supports a plant. The word evokes the idea of "support" or "sustenance" — that which holds something in place and prevents it from falling.
H3657.origine: The word belongs to the family of "kanân" (כָּנַן), which means "vine" or "vineyard." This root evokes the idea of planting and establishing something durable in the soil. The image of the vine — a plant that is cultivated, supported, and protected against the elements and threats — explains the meanings of "support," "stem," and "to protect." It is a concrete word that speaks of an agricultural action, but which biblical poetry uses to describe God's action in establishing and protecting His people.
H3657.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible. It is found in Psalm 80, a song that compares Israel to a vine planted by God in Egypt and transplanted in Canaan. The psalmist asks God to "protect" this vine — that is, to keep it against devastation and external threats. The context shows that it is a prayer for God to defend and support the people He has established, just as one tends to a cultivated plant.
H3657.portee: This word reminds us that God has not only planted His people: He actively supports and protects them. It is an invitation to trust in the one who has established us and watches over us. For the Christian, this evokes the promise that God keeps what He has created in us.

sens: Stringed musical instrument
Musical accompaniment for praise and dance
Symbol of joy and celebration
Mark of the absence of joy when abandoned
H3658.detail:
1. The harp is a musical instrument made of strings stretched over a frame, which are plucked to produce sounds. It is one of the oldest instruments mentioned in the Bible: Jubal, the son of Lamech, is presented as its inventor or the first musician (Genesis 4:21).
2. The harp is primarily used to accompany songs of praise and festive dances during religious celebrations. David has it played when the ark of the covenant enters Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:5), and King Solomon orders it for the house of the Lord (1 Kings 10:12).
3. The harp symbolizes joy, celebration, and thanksgiving to God. The psalmists invoke it to praise the Lord: "Awake, my lute and harp! I will awaken the dawn" (Psalms 108:3).
4. Conversely, when the people are in exile or mourning, they abandon their harp: the captives in Babylon hang their harps on the willows, unable to sing (Psalms 137:2), which shows that this instrument is inseparable from freedom and trust in God.
H3658.origine: The Hebrew word "kinnor" belongs to a family of ancient musical instruments. The name likely reflects the sound produced by this stringed instrument. The harp was known throughout the ancient Near East, both among the Egyptians and the Mesopotamians. In the Hebrew Bible, it is among the favored instruments of worship and sacred music of Israel.
H3658.emploi: The harp is mentioned 41 times in the Hebrew Bible. It appears mainly in the Psalms (where it illustrates praise) and in the accounts of the kings of Israel (where it magnifies the worship of the Temple). David, a musician and poet, plays it to soothe Saul (1 Samuel 16:16-23). The Levites play it during solemn ceremonies of the Temple, notably at the dedication of the ark (2 Chronicles 5:12). The prophets also mention the harp to highlight the abandonment of joy in times of judgment (Isaiah 5:12; 24:8). It is an instrument of the psalmist, the prophet, and the king: it expresses the communion of all Israel with its God.
H3658.portee: The harp is much more than a mere instrument: it represents the authentic joy of the heart turning toward God. Its appearances remind us that true praise comes from one who has known deliverance and grace. When it is silent, it is because sin or distance from God has broken communion. It also teaches us that God deserves not only our words but also our finest art and creation.

sens: king of Judah at the time of the Babylonian exile
H3659.detail: Jeconiah is the name that the prophet Jeremiah gives to King Jehoiachin of Judah. He is a king at the end of the monarchy of Judah, living just before the Babylonian captivity. Jeremiah directly addresses him by comparing him to a precious ring in God's hand (Jeremiah 22:24), then describing him as a despised and broken vessel, rejected along with his offspring (Jeremiah 22:28). After his deportation, his cousin Zedekiah succeeds him on the throne of Judah, still under the authority of the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 37:1).
H3659.origine: The name Jeconiah, or Jehoiachin in Hebrew יְהוֹיָכִין, means "the Lord will establish." He is the same figure that the Bible also calls Coniah in Jeremiah 22:24,28, Shallum in Jeremiah 22:11, and Jeconiah in 1 Chronicles 3:16. This multiplicity of names reflects the different periods of his life and the various contexts in which he is mentioned.
H3659.emploi: Jeconiah is the son of King Jehoiakim and the father of the temple builder Shealtiel. He reigns very briefly over Judah before being deported to Babylon. The prophet Jeremiah addresses him three times in the provided usages: first to remind him that, despite his kingship, he cannot escape God's judgment (Jeremiah 22:24), then to compare him to a worthless object thrown far away (Jeremiah 22:28), and finally to note that Zedekiah reigned in his place after his captivity (Jeremiah 37:1). His fate illustrates the end of Judah's independent monarchy and the fulfillment of divine judgment.
H3659.portee: The fate of Jeconiah reminds the reader that royal power does not escape God's judgment, even when a king seems well established. His exile marks the break in the political continuity of Judah and the entry of the people into captivity, a major event in the history of salvation. However, his descendants, particularly Shealtiel, play a role in the restoration and reconstruction of the temple after the exile, testifying that God does not completely abandon His people.

sens: in this manner, according to what has just been said
consequently, for this reason
in the way that has been described or ordered
H3660.detail:
1. The word designates the manner in which something is done or takes place, referring back to what precedes. It is a logical link: it indicates how an action is performed according to what has just been mentioned. In Ezra 6:13, the Persian authorities "complied" with the king's order — they acted in the prescribed manner, that is, by granting the Jews the freedom to rebuild the temple.
2. The word introduces a consequence or a logical sequence: because something is true, here is how one should act or what follows from it. It conveys the idea of "therefore" or "consequently."
3. The word can also present the way in which something will be done or will unfold, in accordance with a given model or instruction. The action aligns with what has been presented before.
H3660.origine: The word is composed of an Aramaic root that expresses the idea of resemblance or equality: "as, just as." This comparative or conformity particle is typical of the Aramaic used in official documents of the Persian Empire, such as those in the book of Ezra. It clearly connects the action to its antecedent.
H3660.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the book of Ezra (chapters 4 to 6), in a context of royal orders and administrative correspondence between the Persian court and local officials. It serves to show how the authorities execute royal decrees or how responses align with requests. Its usage is typically official and bureaucratic: it clarifies that such action corresponds exactly to such instruction or described situation.
H3660.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of obedience and conformity to the expressed will. For the believer, it invites recognition of how God directs history through the hearts of kings, and how His intentions are faithfully accomplished, even through human power structures.

sens: Levite who participated in the solemn purification of the people under Ezra
H3662.detail: Kenani is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi, tasked with temple service and the religious instruction of Israel. He appears in Nehemiah 9:4 among a group of Levites who ascend the platform to cry out to the Lord during a solemn purification ceremony of the people at the time of the return from exile (the era of Ezra and Nehemiah). His name means "my station," which may evoke his role as a Levite assigned to a specific position in temple service.
H3662.origine: The name Kenani, "my station," reflects the importance of the role assigned to the Levites in Israelite worship. This function of "station" or "post" reminds us that each Levite occupied a designated place in the organization of temple service.
H3662.emploi: Kenani is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 9:4. He is among the Levites who, under the leadership of Ezra and Nehemiah, lead a great assembly of repentance and confession during the return of the exiles to Jerusalem. These Levites are tasked with crying out to God for the people to turn to Him and accept divine purification. His name appears alongside other Levites such as Joshua, Bani, and Kadmiel, demonstrating his equal status among the spiritual leaders of this crucial time.

sens: Levite musician during the time of King David
Chief musician during the transportation of the ark
Administrative officer and judge of Israel
H3663.detail:
1. Kenaniah was a Levite, a member of the tribe dedicated to temple service. He lived during the time of David when the kingdom of Israel was divided between North and South (1 Chronicles 15:22).
2. He led the singers during the grand procession that transported the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. His role was to guide the musicians and singers: he was recognized as particularly gifted in this art (1 Chronicles 15:27).
3. Beyond his musical role, Kenaniah also held important administrative functions. With his brothers, he was responsible for the affairs of the kingdom as a magistrate and judge, administering justice in Israel (1 Chronicles 26:29).
H3663.origine: The name Kenaniah means "God establishes" or "Jehovah establishes," evoking the stability and order that the Lord establishes. This name reflects the belief that God maintains order among His people, which aligns well with Kenaniah's two functions: the harmonious order of worship music and the order of administrative justice.
H3663.emploi: Kenaniah is mentioned three times in Chronicles, all during the time of David. First, he appears as the chief musician during the solemn transportation of the ark, a major event in Israel's history (1 Chronicles 15:22-27). These first two mentions show him at the head of the worship musicians, a ministry of honor that required talent and dedication. Then, in another role, he is presented as an administrative officer of the Izharites (a family of Levites), responsible for the application of the law in Israel (1 Chronicles 26:29). These roles depict a trustworthy figure, esteemed for his integrity and capability in two essential areas: liturgical worship and governance.
H3663.portee: Kenaniah illustrates how God uses faithful servants in varied functions, both spiritual and administrative. His example reminds the believer that service to God is not limited to rituals: it extends to justice, public order, and the wise governance of a community. It is an invitation to seek excellence in all areas entrusted by God, whether liturgical or civil.

sens: to bring together in one place people or objects that are scattered
to accumulate, to pile up goods or wealth
to envelop or cover oneself with something
H3664.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to gather, to bring together what was scattered. David "gathers" the foreigners of the land of Israel to prepare the materials for the Temple (1 Chronicles 22:2), and the Lord "gathers" the exiles of Israel to bring them back to Jerusalem (Psalms 147:2). It also means gathering people by calling them to come together: Esther asks her cousin to "gather" all the Jews of Susa to fast with her (Esther 4:16).
2. The word also means to accumulate, to amass wealth or goods. Ecclesiastes confesses: "I amassed silver and gold, and the treasures of kings and provinces" (Ecclesiastes 2:8). It is to pile up, to put together in quantity.
