3. Rarely, the word can mean to envelop or cover: the water of the sea "gathers" in heaps, that is, accumulates and envelops in reservoirs (Psalms 33:7). This nuance is more passive or reflective.
H3664.origine: The Hebrew verb kanás comes from a root that evokes the idea of gathering, bringing together. The equivalent Aramaic word kénash (H3673) carries the same meaning. The family of the word always shows this idea of putting together, concentrating in one point — whether it be people, objects, or substances.
H3664.emploi: This verb appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Chronicles, Psalms, and Ecclesiastes. It is used to describe concrete actions: gathering workers or materials (1 Chronicles 22:2), collecting offerings in the Temple storerooms (Nehemiah 12:44), or calling people to a decisive moment (Esther 4:16). It can also express spiritual realities: the Lord "gathers" the exiles (Psalms 147:2), restoring unity to the scattered people. In the context of Ecclesiastes, the verb describes the accumulation of wealth and pleasures, showing the vanity of human efforts (Ecclesiastes 2:8).
H3664.portee: This word reminds Christians that unity, whether communal or spiritual, does not arise by chance: it requires an act of gathering. For the scattered Israel, the image of gathering evokes God's faithfulness who does not abandon them. For the reader of Ecclesiastes, the verb warns: accumulating earthly goods is vain. The Church itself, the body of Christ scattered throughout the world, meditates on this reality of gathering by grace.

sens: to voluntarily lower oneself, to acknowledge one's fault and unworthiness before God
to be brought to helplessness, crushed by military defeat or misfortune
to lose one's pride, one's ability to resist
to place someone in a position of inferiority or submission
H3665.detail:
1. To voluntarily lower oneself means to bend pride and acknowledge before God that one has acted wrongly. It is an act of sincere repentance: when Hezekiah "humbled himself" with the people of Jerusalem after his pride, God withheld His anger (2 Chronicles 32:26). It is to accept that one can do nothing without God.

2. To be brought to helplessness means to lose strength in battle or in misfortune, like the Ammonites who were "humiliated" before Israel and could no longer fight (Judges 11:33). The term denotes the physical and moral crushing of a defeated enemy.

3. Losing one's pride and dignity is what God expects from His people: when the Lord saw that the people of Judah "humbled themselves," He refused to destroy them (2 Chronicles 12:7). It is the opposite of rebellion.

4. To place someone in a lower position is the action of God or the victor: the Lord "humbled" all of David's enemies (1 Chronicles 17:10), placing them under his dominion.
H3665.origine: The Hebrew verb kanah originally denotes the action of bending, curving, lowering down. It is related to the idea of losing height, altitude — the opposite of rising. In the Old Testament, this verb combines two meanings: on one hand, the humiliation suffered (being defeated, being stripped), on the other, the voluntary lowering, the humility of heart. Both aim to break pride, to make the soul available to God.
H3665.emploi: The verb kanah appears 32 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the Psalms. It is used primarily in two contexts: first, military humiliation — God submits the enemies of Israel and places them under the dominion of His people (Judges 3:30, 11:33; 1 Samuel 7:13); secondly, personal repentance — when someone humbles themselves before God by acknowledging their guilt, they obtain forgiveness and escape judgment (2 Chronicles 12:7, 32:26, 33:12). In a few passages, the word also describes the subjugation of the people to their enemies as punishment for unfaithfulness (Leviticus 26:41; Psalms 106:42).
H3665.portee: This word teaches believers two lessons. First, that humility before God is not a shameful weakness, but the key to salvation and forgiveness: acknowledging one's fault breaks divine anger and calms the conscience. Second, that God is the only one who truly has power: He alone humiliates enemies and protects His own. It is an invitation to lower pride and to trust in God alone.

sens: what is gathered and wrapped together
a set of goods one takes with oneself
what belongs to someone, their lot or share
H3666.detail: 1. The word denotes a bundle, a bunch, a set of objects closely gathered and tied together — the image of a compact load that one can carry. 2. By extension, it refers to a set of personal belongings, what one possesses and takes with them: their affairs, their luggage. In its only biblical usage (Jeremiah 10:17), the prophet addresses besieged Jerusalem and asks her to take her "bundle," meaning her possessions, her goods. 3. More figuratively, it refers to what belongs to someone, their lot, their share — what characterizes their condition or possession.
H3666.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root evoking the idea of gathering, forming a compact set. It describes the concrete action of making a bundle, tying together disparate things to make a transportable load. It is a practical and concrete term, very rooted in the nomadic or agricultural daily life, where possessing few things and carrying them with oneself was a common reality.
H3666.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible: in Jeremiah 10:17. It is a poetic and expressive term that the prophet uses to evoke the forced exodus, the deportation threatening Jerusalem. By using this image of the "bundle" one takes, Jeremiah makes the imminent catastrophe very concrete and visual: it is not a theological abstraction, but the image of women and children gathering their belongings to go into exile.
H3666.portee: This word reminds us that our material possessions are fragile and temporary. The prophet uses it to confront the people with the reality of judgment: one can only carry what one can hold in their arms. It is an invitation to rethink what truly matters — not our possessions, which can be taken from us, but our faithfulness to God.

sens: geographical region beyond the Jordan, inhabited by the Canaanites before the Israelite conquest
land promised by God to Abraham and his descendants
kingdom occupied by Israel after the exodus from Egypt
H3667A.detail:
1. Canaan is the name of the region located west of the Jordan, in the Levant. It is the territory that the descendants of Canaan, the grandson of Noah, populated before the arrival of the Israelites (Genesis 50:5). Abraham first enters as a foreigner and dwells there (Genesis 12:5), and Jacob also lives there among the indigenous populations (Genesis 37:1).
2. God promises this land to Abraham and his descendants to make it their eternal possession (Exodus 6:4). It is the promised land that the patriarchs dream of but do not possess during their lifetime (Genesis 48:3). This promise runs throughout the history of Israel: Moses sees Canaan from afar before his death (Deuteronomy 32:49).
3. Under the command of Joshua, Israel conquers this land and settles there. The Israelites fight against the Canaanite kingdoms (Judges 4:2-23), take possession of it, and divide it among the tribes (Joshua 14:1). Canaan then becomes the kingdom of Israel and the place of worship to the Lord.
H3667A.origine: Canaan is named after a son of Ham, the son of Noah (Genesis 9:18). In Hebrew, the word means "low land" or "humbled" (it is a land of valleys and plains compared to the surrounding high plateaus). The word refers both to the region and its inhabitants, the Canaanites. When the Israelites conquer the land, Canaan changes status: from the domain of the Canaanites, it becomes the land of God's people.
H3667A.emploi: Canaan appears about eighty times in the Bible, mainly in Genesis where the patriarchs live as foreigners (Genesis 11:31, 45:25). The accounts in Exodus and Numbers designate it as the goal of the exodus: the people freed from Egypt walk forty years toward it (Exodus 16:35, Numbers 13:2). Joshua and the Judges describe the conquest and occupation of the land by Israel (Joshua 14:1, Judges 4:2). The psalms celebrate the promise of this heritage (Psalms 105:11). The word is thus used to refer to both the geographical territory, the divine promised land, and the domain of the people of Israel.
H3667A.portee: Canaan reminds Christians that God does not fulfill His promises vaguely or spiritually, but concretely: He gives His people a land, a territory, a real possession. Canaan also symbolizes the inheritance that God grants to His children. For believers, this earthly promise speaks of the broader promise of rest and possession in God: one enters into what He promises just as Israel had to enter into Canaan with faith and obedience.

sens: historical region of the Levant, promised by God to Abraham and his descendants
trading and merchant people of this region
the entirety of the inhabitants and culture of this land
H3667B.detail: 1. Canaan is primarily the name of the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — the region located between the Mediterranean and the Jordan, which God swore to Abraham's descendants. It is the land that the Israelites conquered under Joshua and inhabited. 2. The word also refers to the peoples who inhabited this region before Israel: traders and merchants known for their commercial exchanges (Ezekiel 16:29 calls the people of Canaan merchants). 3. By extension, Canaan can refer to the entirety of the population and culture of this territory — its inhabitants, the Canaanites, with their religious practices and ways of life.
H3667B.origine: The name Canaan comes from an ancient Semitic root. In Hebrew, the word is related to the idea of commerce and merchant — which explains why the Canaanites were known as traders. The term applies to both the geographical territory and its inhabitants. The derived adjective "Canaanite" (כְּנַעֲנִי) refers to an inhabitant of Canaan or a merchant.
H3667B.emploi: Canaan appears about five times in the provided usages, mainly in the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Zephaniah). The word designates the region as land, but the Bible also emphasizes the commercial aspect of its inhabitants: Ezekiel 16:29 and Hosea 12:8 associate Canaan with merchants and commercial dishonesty. Isaiah 23:8 mentions the merchants of Canaan. Zephaniah 1:11 refers to the merchants of the land. The prophetic context often critiques the commercial and idolatrous practices associated with Canaan.
H3667B.portee: For the believer, Canaan reminds us that God had promised a land to His people — a concrete and geographical promise. It is a sign of God's faithfulness to His commitments. But the Bible also associates Canaan with false gods, immoral practices, and the idolatry that the Canaanites practiced: it warns Israel not to imitate these peoples. Canaan thus embodies both the promised blessing and the spiritual danger of compromise with paganism.

sens: son of Ham and grandson of Noah
H3667G.detail: Canaan is the name of a man who lived during the time of the Patriarchs. He is presented as the son of Ham and the grandson of Noah in the account that follows immediately after the Flood. He is also the father of a numerous lineage: Sidon, Heth, the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. His name appears mainly in Genesis 9, where he is cursed by Noah because of his father Ham's wrongdoing: "Cursed be Canaan! He shall be a servant of servants to his brothers!" (Genesis 9:25). This curse is solemn and repeated, and it profoundly marks the fate of his descendants.
H3667G.origine: The name Canaan (in Hebrew כְּנַעַן) probably means "merchant" or "one who bows down" (from the idea of bending under a burden of commerce). In the Bible, Canaan first designates this ancestor and his descendants, and then by extension the territory populated by his descendants — the land of Canaan — which will become the home of the people of Israel after the exodus from Egypt.
H3667G.emploi: Canaan appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis 9 and 10, and in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He only appears as a name in these genealogical lists; no detailed account of his life is provided. His role is to mark the genealogical link between Noah and Ham on one hand, and the peoples who will inhabit the land of Canaan on the other. The key passage (Genesis 9:25-27) shows that Canaan suffers the curse pronounced by Noah, a curse that affects his descendants and their territorial inheritance.
H3667G.portee: The fate of Canaan illustrates an important biblical lesson: the sin of parents has consequences for the next generation, and the curse can weigh upon a family or people. However, this curse is not presented as absolute or without remission; it places Canaan and his descendants in the history of salvation. The land of Canaan, bearing the name of this cursed ancestor, paradoxically becomes the place where God establishes His covenant with Abraham and his descendants, showing how God transforms even cursed situations into the fulfillment of His promises.

sens: Father of the false prophet Zedekiah during the divided monarchy
Ancestor of a branch of the tribe of Benjamin
H3668G.detail:
1. Kenaana is the father of Zedekiah, a false prophet who served King Ahab of Israel. Zedekiah made iron horns and predicted victory against the Syrians (1 Kings 22:11), seeking to flatter the king with deceitful prophecies. It was this same Zedekiah who struck the prophet Micaiah on the cheek for opposing his predictions (1 Kings 22:24).
2. Kenaana was also an ancestor in the genealogy of Benjamin: son of Bilhan, grandson of Jediael, and great-grandson of Benjamin. He founded a house, meaning he is the origin of an important family branch within the tribe.
H3668G.origine: The name means "merchant" or "trader" in Hebrew, evoking one who engages in commerce or negotiation. It is a name that reflects an activity or profession, common in ancient Hebrew onomastics.
H3668G.emploi: Kenaana appears four times in Scripture, always as the father of Zedekiah, in two parallel passages: the account in 1 Kings 22:11-24 and its equivalent in 2 Chronicles 18:10-23. These passages recount the episode where King Ahab gathers his prophets to know the outcome of a battle against the Syrians. Zedekiah, son of Kenaana, stands out for his spectacular and deceitful commitment alongside other prophets, and then for his violent reaction towards Micaiah, the true prophet who denounces their false prophecies. Kenaana himself never speaks: he is mentioned only to identify his infamous son.
H3668G.portee: This name reminds us that false prophets did not arise from nothing, but were part of family lineages. The story of Zedekiah, son of Kenaana, shows how one can be surrounded by deceptive flattery and violence for daring to speak the truth in God's name. For the believer, it is a call to discern true prophets from impostors, even when the majority approves of them.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, contemporary of the divided monarchy
Son of Bilhan and grandson of Jediael
H3668H.detail: Kénaana is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in Scripture. He is presented as one of the sons of Bilhan (1 Chronicles 7:10), making him the grandson of Jediael and a descendant of Benjamin, the founder of his tribe. His name means "merchant" or "trader," likely evoking a commercial activity. He is the brother of Jeusch, Benjamin, Ehud, Zethan, Tarsis, and Achishachar, all listed in the genealogy of Benjamin.
H3668H.origine: The name Kénaana (כְּנַעֲנָה) means "merchant" or "trader" in Hebrew, derived from the root evoking commerce and exchange. This same name is borne by other biblical characters, notably the father of the false prophet Zedekiah during the time of Ahab, indicating that it was a name used multiple times in Israel's history. The commercial meaning of the name likely reflects the activity or social status of those who bore it.
H3668H.emploi: Kénaana appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:10, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is listed among the sons of Bilhan, in the record of the descendants of Jediael. This mention is part of the account of genealogical records that the chronicler compiled to show the structure and descent of the tribes of Israel, particularly those of the Northern Kingdom after the monarchy's division.

sens: one who buys and sells goods for profit
trader, dealer
one who exploits a sacred place for profit
H3669B.detail:
1. The merchant is one who engages in commerce by buying goods to resell. In Job 40:25, fishermen are mentioned who trade fish and share it among the merchants — these buy the merchandise to distribute or resell it.
2. The term more broadly designates the trader or dealer, active in everyday commerce. The woman in Proverbs 31:24 makes shirts and sells them, and she delivers belts to the merchant — she herself acts as a merchant, or she resells her products to other merchants.
3. By moral extension, the merchant represents one who seeks profit in a place that should be dedicated to God. In Zechariah 14:21, the eschatological vision declares that there will no longer be merchants in the house of the Lord — a critique of those who commercially exploited the Temple, diverting the sanctuary from its true purpose: the worship of God.
H3669B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the same root as "Canaan" (כְּנַעַן), the quintessential trading country. Indeed, the Canaanites and the Phoenicians were renowned throughout the Ancient Near East for their commercial activities. The word thus primarily designates an inhabitant of Canaan, and by metonymy, a merchant — as the Canaanites embodied trade and mercantile exchange in the eyes of the Israelites.
H3669B.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the singular or plural designating merchants. In Job 40:25, it refers to fish merchants. In Proverbs 31:24, it is in a positive economic context where the virtuous woman makes and sells her products. But in Zechariah 14:21, the context becomes critical and eschatological: on the day of judgment and renewal, no merchant — that is, no profiteer — will remain in the Temple. This contrast shows that commerce itself is not condemned, but the exploitation of the sanctuary for gain is abominable.
H3669B.portee: This word challenges the believer regarding the true meaning of what is sacred. The merchants of the Temple, whom Jesus later drove out (John 2:14-16), embody profanation: transforming a house of prayer into a marketplace. The entry invites reflection on how we honor or desacralize places, times, and spiritual practices. It is also a reminder that material profit must never take precedence over worship and communion with God.

sens: woman from Canaan
wife of Simeon, mother of Shaul
H3669G.detail:
1. A woman from Canaan, the land that God promised to Abraham and his descendants. In the time of the Patriarchs, the Canaanites formed the indigenous population of this region, and it was not uncommon for the Israelites to marry women from this people.
2. More specifically, it designates the wife of Simeon (son of Jacob) and mother of Shaul, mentioned in the list of Jacob's sons who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:10). Her personal name is not given: she is identified only by her Canaanite origin. The same person is named in Exodus 6:15, in a similar genealogical context.
H3669G.origine: The Hebrew word "Canaanite" comes from "Canaan," the name of the land stretching from the Mediterranean to the banks of the Jordan. The Canaanites are the inhabitants of this land, and the word applies to their descendants. In Greek, this same word has given "Canaanite." The epithet "Canaanite" emphasizes the ethnic and geographical identity of this woman within the people of Israel that was in formation.
H3669G.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, both times to designate this same woman: in Genesis 46:10, during the migration of Jacob's family to Egypt, and in Exodus 6:15, where the genealogy of Simeon is repeated. She is never named personally, but always referred to by her ethnic background. Her role is modest: she is the mother of Shaul, one of Jacob's grandsons. These two verses are part of genealogical lists that establish the descent of Jacob's sons and the composition of the Israelite family in Egypt.
H3669G.portee: This woman reminds us that the ancestors of Israel married women from neighboring peoples and that the genealogy of Israel includes alliances with other nations. Her integration into the lineage of Simeon shows that belonging to the people of God is transmitted through family, beyond the ethnic boundaries of the time. It also illustrates how God builds His people by welcoming foreigners who adhere to His promise.

sens: to be set aside, rejected to a corner
to disappear from sight, no longer be visible
to be removed, relegated far from someone's presence
H3670.detail:
1. The verb literally evokes the act of being pushed or rejected into a corner, an isolated place. The image is of a person or thing being set aside, relegated far from view. In Isaiah 30:20, the teachers who instruct the people will no longer be "hidden" — that is, relegated to the sidelines, invisible or distant — but the eyes of the people will be able to see them clearly.

2. This verb describes the state of one who is hidden, who disappears from public view. It is less about voluntary concealment than about being rejected or excluded. This is why the context in Isaiah evokes the end of a situation where wisdom and guides seemed inaccessible or hidden from the people.
H3670.origine: The Hebrew root כנף literally means "corner" or "wing" — the idea of an extremity, a limit. In the reflexive form (Niphal), the verb describes the action of finding oneself pushed, relegated to the periphery, out of sight. This family of words everywhere evokes a setting aside, a separation.
H3670.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in the form given to us, in Isaiah 30:20. The context is that of the messianic promise: after anguish and distress (the bread and water of trial), the people will benefit from a clear and immediate divine presence. The teachers who instruct will no longer be "hidden" — relegated far away — but visible and accessible. It is a picture of restoration and renewed closeness with the source of wisdom.
H3670.portee: This passage speaks to the Christian facing trial: it reminds him that even in anguish, God accompanies His people, and that confusion or lack of clarity are not eternal. The day will come when God's wisdom and guidance will no longer be hidden or distant, but evident to the eyes of those who believe. It is a promise of clarity restored after darkness.

sens: Member that birds and certain celestial beings use to fly.
Edge or end of something: hem, flap of clothing, or edge of an object.
Extremity of a region or area of territory.
Protection, refuge offered by someone (image of a mother wing protecting her young).
Strength, speed, or rapid movement (figurative).
H3671.detail:
1. The wing is the member that God gives to birds and flying creatures to move in the air. In Genesis 1:21, He creates all the "winged" birds. Celestial beings, like the cherubim in Ezekiel's vision, also have wings: in Ezekiel 1:6, each had four to move and manifest divine power.
2. The word also refers to the edge of a fabric, the flap of a garment, or the edge of an object. In 1 Samuel 15:27, Saul grabs Elizabeth by the "flap" of his cloak, which tears. The edge of the wings of God's garment also represents His visible boundaries or limits.
3. The wing signifies the extremity of a region or area. In Job 37:3, God's lightning "shines to the ends of the earth." In Psalms 139:9, "taking the wings of the dawn" means reaching the ends of the world where the sun rises.
4. The wing is an image of maternal or divine protection. In Ruth 3:9, she asks Boaz to "spread his wing over her," meaning to take her under his protection. In Psalms 91:4, the psalmist believes that God will cover him "with His wings," keeping him safe from danger.
5. The wing evokes speed and strength of movement: in Proverbs 23:5, wealth "flies away" like the wings of an eagle, suddenly gone. It is the image of something that escapes quickly or unfolds with power.
H3671.origine: The Hebrew word kanâph comes from a root that primarily evokes the movement of flapping and extending. It originally designates the wing of a bird, the part that extends and flaps for flight. By extension, it applies to anything that extends, borders, or terminates something: the hem of a garment, the edge of a piece of furniture, the boundary of a territory. This image of unfolding and extension is at the heart of the word: it produces the idea of protection (motherly wing) and speed (bird's flight).
H3671.emploi: The word kanâph appears 85 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Psalms, Ezekiel, and the historical books. Its major uses are: 1) The wing of birds, ordinary or divine (Genesis 1:21, Ezekiel 1:6 and following); 2) The wing as refuge or protection, an image of divine goodness or care for someone (Ruth 3:9, Psalms 91:4); 3) The wing as the extremity of a region (Job 37:3, Psalms 139:9); 4) The flap or hem of a garment (1 Samuel 15:27). Poetic and prophetic texts mainly use it figuratively, while historical narratives tend to use the material sense.
H3671.portee: This word teaches the believer about God's protection and tenderness. When the Bible speaks of taking refuge "under the wings" of the Lord (Psalms 91:4), it expresses a childlike trust: God envelops His people like a mother bird her young. This image unites divine strength (the bird that flies high and far) and protective softness (the wing that covers and warms). It invites us to seek refuge in God and to experience His security.

sens: Freshwater lake located north of the Jordan Valley, in the Promised Land
H3672G.detail: Kinneret is the ancient name of the lake we know today as the Sea of Galilee. It is a large body of freshwater bordered by hills, traversed by the Jordan River, which marks an important natural boundary in the geography of Canaan. In the historical books of the Bible, this lake is regularly mentioned as a landmark for delineating the territories allocated to the tribes of Israel after the conquest (Numbers 34:11; Deuteronomy 3:17; Joshua 12:3 and 13:27).
H3672G.origine: The name "Kinneret" comes from Hebrew and literally means "harps." This poetic designation is likely inspired by the shape of the lake or the sound of the waves, which the ancient inhabitants compared to the sound of a harp. It is a beautiful example of how biblical peoples named places based on the impression they produced on them.
H3672G.emploi: The term "Kinneret" appears four times in the Old Testament, only in the books of Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua, where it serves as a geographical marker for tracing the borders and possessions of the tribes. It is always referred to as "the Sea of Kinneret" to distinguish this lake from the Mediterranean Sea or the Dead Sea (the Salt Sea). After the biblical period, this name was replaced by other designations, and the lake eventually came to be called "Sea of Galilee" or "Lake of Tiberias."

sens: Fortified city of Israel, located in the region of Naphtali near the Sea of Galilee
Region or district in northern Israel
H3672H.detail: 1. Kinneret is a fortified city in the northern kingdom of Israel, mentioned among the key cities of the tribe of Naphtali. It is located near the Sea of Galilee, in a strategic area of the northern mountains. The name means "harps" in Hebrew, likely related to the shape of the region or the lake. 2. Beyond the city itself, the term also refers to the surrounding region: in 1 Kings 15:20, Ben-Hadad conquers "all Kinneroth," showing that it is a territory, not just a locality.
H3672H.origine: The name Kinneret comes from the Hebrew kinnôr, which means "harp." The exact origin of the link between the name of the instrument and that of the city or region is uncertain: perhaps the relief resembled the shape of a harp, or perhaps the name reflects a local legend. This same Hebrew word kinnôr appears in the Bible to designate the musical instrument that David played, highly valued in Israel.
H3672H.emploi: Kinneret appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a military or administrative context. In Joshua 11:2, it is mentioned during Joshua's conquest of the north as one of the cities of the king of Hazor. In Joshua 19:35, it appears in the list of fortified cities allocated to the tribe of Naphtali. In 1 Kings 15:20, it is conquered by the Arameans under Ben-Hadad, showing that it remained a strategic point in the wars between rival kingdoms. The Sea of Galilee itself is referred to as "the Sea of Kinneret" or "Lake Gennesaret" in other biblical texts.

sens: High-ranking Persian official responsible for the administration of a province
Magistrate or dignitary summoned for an official ceremony
H3673.detail:
1. A satrap is a high-ranking governor in the Persian empire: he administers an entire province on behalf of the king and exercises authority over all subjects living there. It is a prestigious title, reserved for trusted men of the sovereign. In Daniel 3:3, the satraps are summoned along with other dignitaries to attend the dedication of the giant statue erected by Nebuchadnezzar.
2. More broadly, the word refers to any man of power, any advisor or magistrate called to participate in a royal assembly or solemn event. These dignitaries form a council or court around the monarch: in Daniel 3:27, the satraps and governors rush to witness the miracle of the three young men escaping the flames.
H3673.origine: The Aramaic word כְּנַשׁ (k'nash) literally means 'one who assembles' or 'one who gathers': it comes from a root expressing the action of gathering or summoning. It is an administrative term from the Persian empire, borrowed from the political context of the time when the Jewish people lived under Persian domination. The word reflects the hierarchical and centralized organization of this empire.
H3673.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in chapter 3 of the book of Daniel. It specifically designates the high Persian (then Median) officials surrounding the king. In Daniel 3:2, King Nebuchadnezzar summons them to attend the dedication of a golden statue. In Daniel 3:3 and 3:27, they indeed rush and witness the miraculous events. The context is invariably that of an official assembly where royal power is manifested solemnly.
H3673.portee: This word reminds us that God reigns over all earthly powers, even the highest and most prestigious. The satraps, despite their authority, can do nothing against divine protection: in Daniel 3, they witness God's miracle towards His faithful servants. This encourages the reader not to fear the powerful of the world, but to remain faithful to God alone.

sens: person who works with another for the same task or project
companion associated in a business or function
H3674.detail:
1. This word designates a person who collaborates with another in the same work. In Ezra 4:7, the 'colleagues' are Persian and Aramaic officials who together send a letter to King Artaxerxes to oppose the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem. It is an administrative term used to describe people who share the same mission or position.
2. More broadly, it refers to a companion or associate, someone with whom one collaborates in a common task. The context of Ezra shows men of different backgrounds united by a common goal: to influence the king through a written petition.
H3674.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a root meaning 'together' or 'with'. Aramaic was the administrative language of the Persian empire, and this term reflects the vocabulary of royal courts and official offices of the ancient Levant. It is the same word that appears as an Aramaic form in H3675 in the Hebrew nomenclature.
H3674.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:7, an Aramaic text that reports the official correspondence with the Persian king. It is an administrative section of the book of Ezra, entirely in Aramaic, which deals with the obstacles encountered during the rebuilding of the temple after the exile in Babylon. The usage is precise and contextualized: it designates the officials who conspired together against this project.
H3674.portee: This term reminds us that the faith of God's people has often had to face hostility from political authorities. The 'colleagues' of Ezra 4:7 attempted to block God's work through administrative intrigues, but God allowed the temple to be ultimately rebuilt. It is a lesson on perseverance in fulfilling divine will despite obstacles.

sens: Person who works or holds a position alongside another
Member of an official group with a common mission
Associate in an administrative or political responsibility
H3675.detail:
1. The word designates a person who shares a charge or function with another, in a relationship of professional equality. In Ezra 4:9, Rehum and Shimshai are governor and secretary, and the text mentions 'the rest of their colleagues': Persian officers who act together to oppose the rebuilding of the temple.
2. More broadly, it designates members of a delegation or administration who work together. In Ezra 5:6, Tattenai sends a report to the king alongside Shethar-Bozenai and 'their colleagues from Apharsach': all participate together in investigating the construction site in Jerusalem and reporting to the central authority.
H3675.origine: The Aramaic word כְּנָת (ke.nat) comes from a root meaning 'to assemble' or 'to gather'. It expresses the idea of being gathered with others in the same function or task. The form corresponds to the concept of official camaraderie rather than personal friendship: it is a companion in administrative or professional work.
H3675.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the book of Ezra, mainly in chapters 4 to 6, which recount the obstacles to the rebuilding of the temple. It always appears in the plural: 'their colleagues'. The context is always political and administrative: Persian governors, scribes, officers acting collectively either to block the work of the Jews (Ezra 4:9, 4:17, 4:23) or to inspect them (Ezra 5:3, 5:6, 6:6). The word emphasizes that these characters act as a team, with shared responsibility before the king of Persia.
H3675.portee: This word reminds us that everyone in their charge depends on their colleagues and shares the responsibility of common decisions. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to consider those who work or serve alongside them not as rivals, but as companions to whom they must be accountable and with whom they must move forward together in the entrusted mission.

sens: Seat of honor and power, generally royal
Symbol of the authority and reign of a person or a deity
Symbol of divine power and majesty
H3676.detail: 1. The throne is primarily an elevated seat where a king or sovereign sits to display his dignity and exercise his authority: it is a piece of power furniture, more than just a chair. 2. By extension, the word designates royal authority itself, reign, or dominion: 'to lift one's hand against the throne' means to contest the power and sovereignty of the king. 3. In the context of the Eternal (Exodus 17:16), the throne evokes divine majesty, the seat from which God governs the universe and from which His judgments emanate: that is why touching the throne of the Eternal is to attack His very sovereignty.
H3676.origine: This Hebrew word kes is a variant of kisseh (כִּסֵּא), which designates the elevated seat. The root evokes the idea of 'to cover' or 'to conceal', like a seat that protects the one sitting on it. The throne, in antiquity, was the visible symbol of the hidden power of the sovereign. It is a very ancient word, common to Semitic languages to describe the seat of power.
H3676.emploi: The word appears only once in this form in Isaiah and in the provided usages (Exodus 17:16). It is a less common variant than kisseh, which is the standard term for designating the royal or divine throne in the Old Testament. In Exodus 17:16, Moses speaks of 'the hand raised against the throne of the Eternal': this expression means that Amalek has attacked the sovereignty and majesty of God Himself, which will lead to a perpetual war. The context shows that the throne is not a material object, but the living symbol of divine power.
H3676.portee: Recognizing the throne of the Eternal is to accept that God reigns sovereignly over all things. This passage reminds the reader that opposing God or despising His power has lasting consequences and that divine vengeance continues from generation to generation. It is a call to respect God's absolute authority in the history of the people.

sens: The moon when it is fully illuminated, at the midpoint of the lunar cycle
The moment or period of the month when the moon is thus illuminated
A liturgical or festive date marked by this lunar phase
H3677.detail:
1. The full moon is the moment in the lunar cycle when the entire face of the moon visible from the earth is illuminated by the sun. It is the opposite of the new moon, when it is invisible. In Psalms 81:4, the full moon is mentioned as the time of a solemn feast of Israel, alongside the new moon.
2. The term also designates the period or interval of time that corresponds to this phase — about two weeks after the new moon. In Proverbs 7:20, "at the new moon" means "the day of the new moon" or "next month"; by symmetry, the full moon is a moment in the calendar that could be counted to date a departure or a return.
3. In the religious context of Israel, the full moon marked a festive or cultic occasion: it structured the liturgical calendar and the assemblies of the people, as seen in Psalms 81:4.
H3677.origine: The Hebrew word kèsèh comes from a root meaning "to cover" or "to fill." The full moon is literally the moon "covered" or "filled" with light — fully illuminated — in contrast to the new moon which is hidden. The word appears rarely in biblical Hebrew (only twice), but it clearly designates this well-known lunar phase, important for marking times and seasons.
H3677.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 81:4, it accompanies a call to blow the trumpet at the new moon and at the full moon, during a feast of Israel — probably the Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot), which began at the new moon of the seventh month. In Proverbs 7:20, it designates the moment when an adulterous man will not return home until the full moon (that is, long after his departure). In both cases, the word refers to a specific point in the lunar calendar, easy to recognize and memorize for dating events.
H3677.portee: The full moon reminds us that the biblical calendar was lunar, not solar: the feasts and important moments of life were regulated by the phases of the moon, visible to all. This underscores how Israel's faith was rooted in God's created order, which everyone could read in the sky. The mention of the full moon in a festive context also shows that the gatherings of the people before God marked time and sanctified the natural cycle.

sens: Elevated seat, generally adorned, on which a king or deity sits
Position of power, royal authority, or sovereignty
Kingdom or dominion of a king
Place of judgment and justice
Seat of God in His glory and majesty
Duration or stability of a dynasty's power
H3678G.detail:
1. The throne is primarily a physical seat, but it is not just a piece of furniture: it is a seat of honor, richly adorned, where the one who governs takes their place (1 Kings 10:18-19 describes Solomon's magnificent throne, with its backrest, armrests, and lions). This seat visually elevates the king above his people and reminds them of his unique status.

2. The term also designates royal power itself, the dignity and authority of the king. When we speak of "setting someone on the throne" (1 Kings 1:47), we are not only thinking of the physical act but of the transfer of power: it is to establish someone in the royal function with all its rights and responsibilities.

3. By extension, the throne represents the kingdom or dominion of a dynasty — the house of David, for example. The prophecies that promise that David's throne will last forever (2 Samuel 7:13-16) speak of the continuation of royal power through generations.

4. In the context of the kings of Israel and Judah, the throne is also the place from which justice flows: judges and kings sit on thrones to render justice (Psalms 122:5 speaks of thrones for justice, the house of David).

5. The Psalms speak of God's throne as the symbol of His glory and absolute dominion: God reigns on the cherubim (Psalms 93:2, 97:2). It is a throne of majesty, eternal and unshakeable, far greater than any human throne.

6. The throne also expresses the permanence and stability of power. The promises of the throne "established forever" mean that the royal lineage will endure, that the covenant with David will not be broken.
H3678G.origine: The Hebrew word קִסֵּא (kissé) likely comes from a root meaning to sit or remain seated. It is related to other Semitic words meaning "seat." The word evokes the idea of stability and an established position: the one who sits on a throne does not easily change places. This is why the throne becomes the symbol of enduring power and recognized authority.
H3678G.emploi: The word "throne" appears more than 110 times in the Old Testament, especially in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles), the Psalms, and the prophets. The usages vary according to context: sometimes it is a concrete object (the description of Solomon's throne in 1 Kings 10), sometimes it is the abstract power ("to set someone on the throne"). A very frequent usage concerns messianic promises: David's throne is promised as perpetual, which foreshadows Christ. God Himself "reigns on a throne" in the poetry of the Psalms, where the divine throne is immaterial but absolutely real. The word also applies to pagan kings (Pharaoh's throne, in Genesis 41:40) and to the thrones of human judges (Psalms 122:5).
H3678G.portee: For a believer, the word "throne" teaches that true power is not that of men, however impressive it may be: only God's throne is stable and eternal. The promises of David's throne, read in light of the New Testament, point to Christ seated at the right hand of the Father — the king whose reign will never end. This word invites the Christian to place their trust not in earthly authorities, but in God's sovereignty and in the dignity of the risen and exalted Christ.

sens: Seat where a king or a person of power sits
Place where authority is exercised and justice is rendered
Symbol of royalty and power
Royal residence or palace
H3678H.detail:
1. The throne is primarily a seat, but not just any seat: it is the elevated seat where a king sits to show himself to his subjects and govern. In 1 Kings 7:7, Solomon builds "the porch of the throne" as a solemn space intended to impress and remind who commands.
2. The throne is not just a piece of furniture: it is the center of power and justice. The king renders his judgments there, receives petitions, and manifests his authority. This is why it is referred to as "the porch of judgment" to designate the same space.
3. In the Bible, the throne represents royalty itself, royal dignity, the right to command. To possess a throne is to be a king; to sit on the throne is to exercise power.
4. The throne can also designate the royal court or palace, the center of government where the king and his advisors reside and act.
H3678H.origine: The Hebrew word kisseh comes from a root that evokes the idea of "to cover" or "to hide" — perhaps because the throne was topped with a canopy or baldachin that covered and isolated it. The word belongs to the family of royal terms: it designates what elevates and separates the king from ordinary people. In Greek, the New Testament uses the word "throne" (thronos) for heavenly thrones, recalling that this Hebrew term also had a spiritual resonance.
H3678H.emploi: The word "throne" (kisseh) appears few times in the provided passages, but its use in 1 Kings 7:7 is revealing: it designates the porch of judgment that Solomon built, that is, the political and judicial space of the king. It is there that the king renders justice and manifests his power. The context shows that a throne is never just a decorative object: it is an instrument of power, a place where royal authority is exercised and major decisions are made.
H3678H.portee: For the believer reading this passage, the throne reminds us that political power must be exercised in the service of justice. Solomon builds a splendid throne, but it is to render judgment — to remind us that authority is legitimate only if it protects the weak and condemns iniquity. It is an image that invites reflection on the responsibility of those who govern.

sens: Seat or piece of furniture on which one sits, generally of fine craftsmanship or intended for an important person
Seat of honor or power, of the judge or king, symbol of his authority
Dignity, power, or authority exercised by a person, notably a sovereign
H3678I.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a concrete piece of furniture: a seat, a chair, a stool. In 2 Kings 4:10, it simply refers to a seat among the furnishings of a room. It is a material object on which one sits, nothing more mysterious.

2. However, this seat often takes on particular significance: it is that of power. In 1 Samuel 1:9 and 4:13, the priest Eli "was sitting on a seat" — it was not just any piece of furniture, but the place that marked his role as a religious leader. When Haman "placed his seat above all the officials" (Esther 3:1), it is indeed a physical chair, but it symbolizes that he is elevated above others.

3. The word eventually comes to designate the office, the dignity itself, the power without the object. "To place someone's seat" means to entrust him with authority, to give him power. This is the figurative sense: the seat represents all the authority and responsibility of a function.
H3678I.origine: The Hebrew word כִּסֵּא (kisséh) likely comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or supporting. The word is related to ancient Semitic terms for "seat" or "throne." Similar words can be found in Aramaic and Arabic. The Hebrew word is concrete in origin — it simply designates the piece of furniture on which one sits — but biblical Hebrew has imbued it with political and religious significance, to the point that it eventually signifies authority and office itself.
H3678I.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the provided texts. It is first found in ancient historical accounts: Eli the priest (1 Samuel 1:9 and 4:13, 4:18), then in other contexts (the room of a prophet in 2 Kings 4:10, Persian administration in Nehemiah 3:7, the court of King Ahasuerus in Esther 3:1). In these early uses, the word almost always designates a concrete piece of furniture associated with a responsibility: the seat of the judge, the king, or the governor. Over time, and especially among the prophets, the word shifts towards the sense of dignity and power: placing someone on the throne means giving him authority. The uses show this progression from the concrete (the furniture) to the figurative (the power).
H3678I.portee: Understanding this word helps to grasp how the Bible links authority to a physical and symbolic reality. The throne is never a pure abstraction: it is a visible piece of furniture, a specific place, that manifests the power of the one who sits there. For the believer, this reminds us that all power comes from a place assigned by God, and that authority is always tied to a concrete responsibility towards those being governed.

sens: inhabitant or native of Chaldea, a region of Babylon
member of the learned class of priests, magicians, or astrologers of Babylon
H3679.detail:
1. The Chaldean is primarily a person from Chaldea, a region located in Babylon (present-day southern Iraq). Thus, Nebuchadnezzar, the great king of Babylon who conquered Jerusalem, is referred to as "the Chaldean" in Ezra 5:12, to denote his origin and political identity.
2. The term also designates the class of learned men, priests, magicians, and astrologers of Babylon, renowned for their knowledge in occult sciences and astrology. These men formed the intellectual and religious elite of Babylon, and the Bible mentions them as the king's advisors.
H3679.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew kasdi (כַּשְׂדִּי), itself borrowed from Chaldea (H3778), which etymologically means "clod-breakers" (those who break clods of earth), likely an allusion to the farmers from this region. It is a geographical and ethnic term that has gained connotations of knowledge and magic.
H3679.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond (Ezra 5:12) to qualify Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon who destroyed the temple of Jerusalem and deported the people of Judah. Here, "Chaldean" emphasizes both the foreign origin of the conqueror and his political power. Elsewhere in the Bible, the Chaldeans are often mentioned as the astrologers and diviners of the royal palace, representing the worldly wisdom and magical practices of Babylon in contrast to the wisdom of God.
H3679.portee: Recognizing that Nebuchadnezzar is a Chaldean reminds us that God allowed a foreign power to punish His unfaithful people. This word also evokes the contrast between the false wisdom of the Babylonian scholars and the true wisdom of God — an important theme for the exiles who had to resist the allure of Babylonian culture.

sens: Place something on a surface to cover it entirely or partially
Hide, conceal something or someone
Dress, clothe, adorn
Completely cover, submerge, overwhelm
Forgive, keep silent about a fault or sin
H3680.detail:
1. To cover means primarily to place something on another surface to cover it: one covers milk with a cloth, one covers a dead body with a mantle (Genesis 9:23), one covers the entrails of a sacrificed animal with fat (Leviticus 3:3).
2. It also means to hide, conceal so that no one sees: Rebekah covers her face so that she is not recognized (Genesis 24:65), Ezekiel covers his face so that his eyes do not see (Ezekiel 12:12).
3. To cover can mean to dress or clothe: in the instructions for the tabernacle, one covers the altar and its objects with fabrics to preserve them (Numbers 4:5 and following).
4. The word also designates a total and overwhelming covering: the waters of the flood cover all the high mountains (Genesis 7:19), the locusts cover the land of Egypt (Exodus 10:5).
5. In a spiritual and moral sense, to cover a fault means to forgive it, not to recall or disclose it: he who covers a fault seeks love (Proverbs 17:9).
H3680.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּסָה (kasah) comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of veiling, obscuring. Words of the same family in Hebrew all denote the act of hiding or covering. This root is very common in the Bible and regularly describes very concrete situations (a garment, a shelter) as well as more spiritual images (the erasure of sin, divine forgiveness).
H3680.emploi: The verb "to cover" appears 149 times in the Hebrew Bible and carries several nuances depending on the context. First, it describes very material and everyday acts: one covers a pit to fill it (Deuteronomy 23:13), one covers oneself with a garment for protection or concealment. Then, it is used in the rituals of the tabernacle and worship: one covers the altar, the sacred instruments (Numbers 4 passim), the cloud covers the tabernacle (Numbers 9:15-16). It also designates a massive and overwhelming action: the waters of the flood cover the earth, the plagues of Egypt cover the land. Finally, the verb takes on a moral and spiritual sense: to cover a fault means to forgive or not to disclose it (Proverbs 17:9), and by extension, God covers our sins.
H3680.portee: Understanding this word helps the believer grasp how the Bible expresses both the concrete action of hiding or protecting and the spiritual mystery of forgiveness. When we read that God "covers" our sins, we glimpse the biblical image of a veil cast over our faults: not their complete erasure, but their concealment, their non-imputation. This word also opens up the gratuity of forgiveness: he who covers another's fault without recalling it shows the love of Christ.

sens: fabric or material that covers something
veil, protective wrap
H3681.detail:
1. Fabric or material intended to cover and protect an object: it is an outer covering that envelops a precious or fragile thing. In the tabernacle, the priests were to place a covering of dolphin skins over the ark of the covenant (Numbers 4:6) and over the altar (Numbers 4:14) to transport and preserve them during the people's journey in the desert.
2. Figuratively, that which envelops, hides, or protects something: a protective layer, visible or invisible, that preserves what is underneath.
H3681.origine: The Hebrew word kasuy comes from the root kasah, which means "to cover" or "to hide." It is a passive participle that literally means "that which is covered" or "that which covers." The family of this root expresses the action of putting a veil over something, hiding it, or protecting it.
H3681.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, only in Numbers 4, in the instructions regarding the transport of the tabernacle objects. It specifically designates the material protections — dolphin skins and fabrics — intended to envelop the ark of the covenant and the altar during the people's movements. It is a very specific term, related to worship and the preservation of sacred objects.
H3681.portee: This "covering" reminds us that holy things required special protection, a separation from the profane. It symbolizes the importance of preserving, respecting, and carefully transporting what is consecrated to God. For the believer, it also evokes the idea that our spiritual life needs to be protected and preserved.

sens: garment or fabric that covers the body
veil that hides or conceals
protection against cold or bad weather
H3682.detail:
1. Garment or fabric that covers the body — the word primarily designates anything that envelops and protects the skin. When Moses forbids keeping a poor man's cloak as a pledge, he calls it a "covering" (Exodus 22:27), as it is the garment he wears at night to sleep. Similarly, the fringes that the Hebrews sew onto their garments are ornaments of "covering" (Deuteronomy 22:12).
2. Veil that hides or conceals — the word can also refer to that which masks, renders invisible, or forgotten. When Abimelech gives a thousand pieces of silver to Sarah, he calls them a "veil" over her eyes, meaning something that will erase the affront committed (Genesis 20:16). It is an image: the money acts as a veil that covers the shame.
3. Protection against cold or bad weather — the covering also protects from cold and nakedness. The poor who spend the night without a "covering" shiver in the cold (Job 24:7), while the abode of the dead itself, in its bare and resource-less reality, has no "veil" to hide from God's eyes (Job 26:6).
H3682.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to cover, to hide." It is related to the idea of protection, concealment, and veiling. This is why "covering" designates both the concrete garment that envelops the body and the abstract veil that hides from view or erases the memory of a fault.
H3682.emploi: The word appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the laws of Moses and in the poems of Job. It is used first in the literal sense: the cloak, the night garment that covers and warms (Exodus 22:27; Job 24:7). It also takes on a figurative sense: that which covers nakedness or shame — thus the pieces of silver given to Sarah act as a "veil" thrown over the affront (Genesis 20:16). Finally, it expresses that which hides from view: even the abode of the dead does not escape God's eyes because it has no "veil" (Job 26:6). The word thus applies to both material needs and to modesty or guilt.
H3682.portee: This word reminds us that God cares about the concrete life of the poor: He guarantees them the necessary covering for sleeping (Exodus 22:27). It also shows that nothing, not even death or secrecy, can hide from God; He sees beyond all veils (Job 26:6). For the believer, the covering thus becomes a symbol of both divine protection and absolute transparency before God.

sens: to slice, detach a part of a plant or object by separating it from the rest
to destroy or annihilate something (figurative sense)
H3683.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the physical action of cutting: sectioning a branch, a shrub, or a thorn by slicing it. It is the concrete gesture of the lumberjack or gardener. However, in the Bible, it mostly applies to destruction, often of lands ravaged by divine wrath (Psalms 80:17 speaks of the vine "cut down" by judgment).
2. Figuratively, "to cut" means to annihilate, make disappear, strike down. Isaiah 33:12 uses the image of dry thorns "cut down" and burned in the fire to speak of the judgment that consumes nations: it is a total and irreversible destruction, the annihilation of that which opposes God.
H3683.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of sectioning, cutting cleanly. It belongs to the family of verbs of destruction and separation. The basic image is that of a blade that cuts, of a knife or sickle that separates a part from the whole. This verb literally translates the physical action, but it is very often used in contexts of divine judgment to signify annihilation.
H3683.emploi: This verb appears only 2 times in the Hebrew Bible, both with the meaning of "to cut" or "to destroy." In Psalms 80:17, it describes the vine of Israel ravaged and "cut down" by the fire of divine judgment — an image of devastation. In Isaiah 33:12, the nations that oppose God are compared to "cut down" and burned thorns: the verb emphasizes total destruction. In both cases, the context is that of judgment: God who cuts, who eliminates, who annihilates what rebels against Him.
H3683.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment is not a mere correction, but a radical separation from sin and rebellion. The image of "cutting" suggests that God does not tolerate iniquity indefinitely: He cuts, He destroys, He allows to remain only what truly belongs to Him. For the believer, it is a call not to harden against God, for the judgment that "cuts" is certain.

sens: one who lacks sense, discernment, and wisdom
one who acts without considering the consequences of their actions
one who despises correction and refuses instruction
one who delights in pride and self-sufficiency
H3684.detail:
1. The fool is primarily one who lacks a sense of reality, who does not understand what is happening around them. It is a lack of perception: as Psalm 49:11 states, the fool will perish just as surely as the wise, even though both believe they can keep their riches. They have not grasped the essential.
2. Secondly, the fool acts without thinking: they do not consider the consequences of their actions. Proverbs 13:16 contrasts them with the prudent man who "acts with knowledge" — the fool, on the other hand, "displays folly," speaking and acting impulsively. Ecclesiastes 4:5 shows them folding their arms in idleness, destroying their own flesh: they lack a sense of consequences.
3. The fool also rejects all correction: they refuse to learn. Proverbs 15:20 depicts a foolish son who despises his mother — one who does not even receive wisdom from the family home. They do not want to listen.
4. Finally, the fool is often puffed up with pride: they elevate themselves above what they are. Proverbs 26:8 states that giving honors to a fool is like "putting a stone in a sling" — it is giving them what they cannot bear, and they will misuse it.
H3684.origine: The Hebrew word קְּסִיל (kesil) comes from a root that evokes the idea of closure, insensitivity. The fool is one who has a heart closed to wisdom, who does not want to see or hear. It is a stable character trait, a way of life. This word belongs to the vocabulary of biblical wisdom, where it is constantly opposed to the "wise" (חָכָם, hakham) and the "prudent" (עָרוּם, arum).
H3684.emploi: The word appears 69 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the wisdom books: especially in Proverbs (50 occurrences) and Ecclesiastes (14), and also in the Psalms. It is a key term in sapiential language. Proverbs unfolds all the contours of the foolish character: their impulsivity, insolence, refusal of correction, inaction, and taste for conflict. Ecclesiastes, on the other hand, emphasizes the absurdity of the fool's existence compared to that of the wise: despite all their folly, both die. The term paints less of an isolated act than a posture, a way of being in front of life and divine wisdom.
H3684.portee: The fool in Proverbs is not merely an ignorant person, but one who willfully rejects wisdom and instruction. This portrait challenges the reader: am I one who listens, learns, and changes course? Or am I one who closes themselves off to correction, who acts without considering the consequences? The wisdom books do not pass definitive judgment; they offer the reader a mirror and the opportunity to turn towards a better path.

sens: Constellation of stars visible in the night sky
Group of celestial bodies arranged in the shape of a hunter
Symbol of God's creative power
H3685G.detail:
1. Orion is a constellation, that is, a group of stars that can be easily recognized in the night sky. In Job 9:9, God is described as the one who "created the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades," showing that Orion is a well-known celestial formation to the ancient Israelites.
2. The constellation of Orion traditionally represents a hunter, with its stars arranged in a distinctive pattern that the peoples of the Middle East could identify. Job 38:31 speaks of "loosening the cords of Orion," using the image of cords to evoke the ties that hold together the stars of this constellation.
3. In the three passages where it appears, Orion is never isolated: it is always mentioned alongside the Bear or the Pleiades, and always in a context that recalls God's power over the universe (Job 9:9, Amos 5:8). It thus becomes a visible sign of divine dominion over creation.
H3685G.origine: The Hebrew word késsil literally means "the fool" or "the foolish one," a meaning that derives from an ancient root denoting stupidity. The ancients applied this name to the constellation of Orion, probably because the hunter represented by these stars was seen as a ridiculous or unfortunate character in surrounding mythologies. The word thus emphasizes irony: what men mock or consider insignificant (a mere mythological figure) is actually a majestic creation of God.
H3685G.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in sapiential or prophetic discourses. In Job 9:9 and 38:31, it is mentioned in God's words to Job to remind him of the vastness and magnificence of the created work: these stars escape human understanding and any attempt at control. In Amos 5:8, the prophet invokes it to show that the one who shapes Orion and the Pleiades is the same who transforms darkness into light and who controls the waters: it is a proclamation of the Lord's universal sovereignty. In all three cases, Orion functions as a celestial wonder that testifies to divine creative power.
H3685G.portee: Orion invites the believer to contemplate God's greatness through the heavens. These passages remind us that we inhabit a vast and splendid universe, shaped by an all-powerful and wise hand. In the face of these distant constellations, we discover our smallness and that of our earthly concerns, which should humble us and inspire us to grateful worship.

sens: Grouping of stars visible in the night sky
Set of celestial bodies forming a recognizable figure
H3685H.detail:
1. The word refers to a group of stars that are seen together in the sky: this is what we call a constellation. In Isaiah 13:10, on a day of divine judgment, the "stars" of heaven will cease to shine along with the stars, showing that even these celestial groupings will lose their light.
2. More broadly, it can evoke any remarkable astral ensemble or figure traced by the stars in the night: the image evokes the order and beauty of the sky that God has created.
H3685H.origine: The Hebrew word כְּסִיל (kesil) comes from a root that suggests the idea of "forming," "giving shape." In ancient thought, the constellations are these "forms" that the stars draw together in the sky. The same family of words evokes what is formed or assembled. It is the term used in the Hebrew Bible to speak of these groups of stars that the ancients recognized and to which they gave names.
H3685H.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 13:10. It is set in a context describing the "day of the Lord," a moment when the heavens themselves will be shaken: the stars will no longer shine, the constellations will disappear from view, the sun and moon will lose their brightness. This passage uses the word to emphasize the cosmic scope of divine judgment — nothing that illuminates the sky will escape this upheaval. It is a technical term to designate these celestial formations, used only once by the prophet to reinforce the image of universal catastrophe.
H3685H.portee: This verse invites the reader to contemplate the greatness of divine creation and, at the same time, its temporary nature before the hand of God. If even the stars, as stable and eternal as they seem, can be obscured on the day of judgment, this reveals the absolute sovereignty of the Lord over all things and calls us to place our trust not in the stability of the visible world, but in the One who governs it.

sens: City in the south of Judah
H3686.detail: Kesil is a small city in the southern part of Judea, mentioned in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah. It is located very far south in the territory of Judah, about 25 kilometers southwest of Beersheba, one of the main cities in the region. Biblical geographers believe that Kesil may be identical to Bethul, another name for this same locality.
H3686.origine: The name Kesil comes from a Hebrew word meaning "foolish" or "fool." It is a particular name given to this city in the south of Judah, probably because of its location or an event that gave it this name in antiquity.
H3686.emploi: Kesil appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Joshua. It is listed among the cities that God distributes to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. It is mentioned between Eltholad and Hormah, two other small towns in the Negev, the desert region of southern Judah. This list shows how the conquered territory was divided among the different tribes of Israel.

sens: Lack of wisdom and common sense
Unreasonable and irrational behavior
Willful insensitivity to the truth and order of God
H3687.detail:
1. Folly is primarily the absence of wisdom, a lack of discernment and common sense in understanding things. It is not seeing or refusing to see what is evident and true. In Proverbs 9:13, the foolish woman represents one who ignores or despises instruction.

2. It is also unreasonable behavior: acting without thinking, without weighing the consequences, like someone who refuses to listen to wise counsel. This folly is not a disease, but a choice.

3. More profoundly, in the Bible, folly is a kind of closing off to God and His wisdom: it is the willful blindness to divine truth, the attitude of one who lives as if God does not exist or does not matter.
H3687.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root kessilut, related to the idea of stupidity and lack of sense. In biblical tradition, folly is always opposed to wisdom (hokmah). While wisdom consists of knowing God and living according to His order, folly is the refusal of that knowledge.
H3687.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 9:13. It describes the foolish woman, an allegorical figure that symbolizes everything that distances one from divine wisdom. This unique occurrence in Proverbs shows that the main theme of the book is indeed wisdom versus folly.
H3687.portee: This word calls the reader to examine their own life: do we listen to God's wisdom and instruction, or do we refuse to hear it? Folly is not an excuse; it is a choice. Growing in wisdom means accepting to be taught by God and to change our behavior according to His truth.

sens: Lack of wisdom and judgment
Acting while ignoring the truth of God
Adopting false beliefs or vain practices
H3688.detail:
1. To be foolish means to lack common sense and discernment regarding what truly matters. It is acting without considering the consequences or the truth. In Jeremiah 10:8, those who make idols are called "foolish": they believe that crafted wood can be a god, which is absurd.
2. To be foolish also means to reject or ignore what God has revealed. The context of Jeremiah shows that folly consists of worshiping mute gods while the true God speaks.
3. This verb denotes willful blindness to the truth: preferring a pleasant lie to a difficult reality, or persisting in error despite the evidence. It is a moral as well as an intellectual folly.
H3688.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of turning away, deviating from the right path. Biblical folly is never simply a lack of intelligence, but rather a refusal or inability to recognize God and His wisdom. The word is related to Hebrew terms that denote other forms of foolishness or moral deviation.
H3688.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 10:8. The prophet denounces the idolaters who trust in wooden statues. To be foolish, in this unique passage, is to believe that man-made objects can be gods. This unique occurrence shows that biblical folly is primarily religious: it consists of placing one's trust elsewhere than in God and preferring nothingness to divine reality.
H3688.portee: This word calls the reader to reflect on the foundation of their beliefs. The Bible considers any trust placed in idols, wealth, or human plans that ignore God to be folly. Recognizing God's wisdom and living according to His word is not an option among others, but the only reasonable and true path.

sens: The area of the belly or loins, between the ribs and hips
The fat surrounding the kidneys in an animal
The assurance, the confidence placed in something
Folly, lack of judgment
H3689.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the part of the human or animal body located between the ribs and the pelvis, that is, the flank or belly. It is one of the areas closest to the heart and the entrails, the seat of emotion. In Leviticus 3:4, the "flanks" covered with fat are mentioned during the sacrifice: the fat that covers the kidneys.
2. In the sacrificed animal, the word particularly refers to the layer of fat that surrounds the kidneys and liver. These very fatty parts were burned on the altar (Leviticus 7:4).
3. By a common image in Hebrew, what is "strong in the flanks" becomes the seat of trust and assurance. The flank represents stability, the strength one feels within oneself. In Psalms 78:7, it is about placing one's trust in God, not in oneself.
4. Conversely, the "folly" of the flanks means the absence of moral solidity, the lack of common sense (Ecclesiastes 7:25). It is an inner weakness that manifests itself through poor decisions.
H3689.origine: The Hebrew word כֶּסֶל comes from a root that first evokes fleshiness, the fleshy part of the body. Over time, "to trust in one's flanks" has taken on the meaning of "to rely on oneself" or more broadly, "to have confidence." Where there is fat, there is apparent strength; but this carnal confidence, according to the Bible, is often an illusion, hence the shift towards "folly" and "foolish assurance."
H3689.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible. The sacrificial uses (Leviticus 3:4, 3:10, 3:15, 4:9, 7:4) place it in a material and concrete context: the flank of the offered animal. Over time, the word has acquired spiritual meanings. In Psalms and Job, it designates the trust or assurance that humans place in themselves or in God. Job 8:14 and 31:24 warn against trust that rests on carnal goods. Psalms 78:7 and Proverbs 3:26 invite one to place their trust not in oneself but in God. Finally, Ecclesiastes 7:25 speaks of the folly of the flanks, that is, unreasonable assurance.
H3689.portee: This word teaches Christians where to place their security. The Bible uses it to show that trust in oneself, in one's riches, or in physical strength is folly: it is a flank that does not hold. It calls us to transfer our assurance to God alone, who is a solid and eternal foundation. Behind this vocabulary of flesh and fat lies a lesson about the heart: where does your trust reside?

sens: Solid support, firm assurance in someone or something
Security provided by certainty — or conversely, false assurance based on illusion
H3690.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a firm assurance, a reliable support upon which one can depend. In Job 4:6, Eliphaz asks Job: "Is not your fear of God your confidence?" — he speaks of that unshakeable trust that comes from a relationship with God.
2. However, the word can also describe a deceptive assurance, misplaced trust — the folly of one who relies on emptiness. In Psalms 85:9, the Lord warns: "Let them not turn back to folly," meaning this blind trust in false gods or in their own wisdom.
H3690.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of leaning on something, resting upon it. It is the image of a person leaning on a staff for support, or placing their weight on a reliable friend. Depending on whether one leans on God or on nothingness, trust becomes strength or folly.
H3690.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 4:6, it denotes legitimate trust, the kind inspired by the fear of God — an assurance rooted in justice and integrity. In Psalms 85:9, it takes on a critical sense: the folly of returning to false supports instead of relying on the peace that God offers. Both uses illuminate the same concept: trust is only valuable if it rests on a solid foundation, that is, on God.
H3690.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine the true source of their trust. Do they rely on God and His integrity, or are they seduced by false supports — wealth, reputation, worldly wisdom? True faith consists of placing one's assurance in the one who alone is reliable.

sens: ninth month of the Hebrew calendar, corresponding to November-December
H3691.detail: 1. Kislev is the ninth month of the civil year according to the Hebrew calendar. It roughly corresponds to our November-December and encompasses the transition from autumn to winter. It is an important month in the history of Israel: in Nehemiah 1:1, Nehemiah is in Susa when he receives news from Jerusalem in the month of Kislev; in Zechariah 7:1, it is on the fourth day of Kislev that the prophet Zechariah receives a word from the Lord.
H3691.origine: The name Kislev comes from the Hebrew word meaning "trust" or "assurance." Although the exact origin of the month's name is debated, this primary meaning may recall a time of security or completed harvest. It is one of the month names that reflects the ancient Hebrew tradition of naming periods of the year according to events or states related to the seasonal cycle.
H3691.emploi: Kislev appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the post-exilic books. In Nehemiah 1:1, it marks the moment when Nehemiah learns of the deplorable state of Jerusalem, which triggers his prayer and ultimately his mission of reconstruction. In Zechariah 7:1, it situates a prophetic revelation in the context of events following the exile. These two occurrences testify to the importance of this month in the post-exilic period and the biblical text's care to precisely date significant events.

sens: father of Elidad, prince of the tribe of Benjamin
H3692.detail: Kislon is a man from the time of the Exodus and the wilderness. He is the father of Elidad, who was chosen as prince of the tribe of Benjamin to participate in the division of the land of Canaan (Numbers 34:21). This is the only mention of Kislon in Scripture.
H3692.origine: The name means "trust" in Hebrew, evoking solidity and assurance. His son Elidad bears a name that means "God is my father," thus expressing trust in divine help.
H3692.emploi: Kislon appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 34:21, where he is named as the father of Elidad. At that moment, Moses designates the leaders of the tribes who will be responsible for distributing the territory of Canaan among the families of Israel. Kislon thus represents a generation of fathers whose sons were raised to serve in important roles for God and the people.

sens: City in the territory of Judah
Place marking a border crossing
H3693.detail:
1. Kesalon is a city located in the mountainous region of northern Judah, about 16 kilometers west of Jerusalem. It marks an important point on the northern border of the tribal territory of Judah (Joshua 15:10).
2. The name "Kesalon" literally means "hopes" in Hebrew, a poetic image for this strategic location. The city is also known as Mount Jearim and served as a geographical landmark to delineate the lands assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of Canaan.
H3693.origine: The name Kesalon derives from a Hebrew root evoking hope or trust. This place also bears the alternative name Jearim ("forests"), suggesting a site in a wooded and mountainous region of Judea. Both names reflect the geographical and symbolic characteristics of the territory during the conquest period.
H3693.emploi: Kesalon appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:10, where it is included in the description of the borders of the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. This passage lists the geographical landmarks that marked the boundaries of the tribal territory. Kesalon served as a crossing point between Beth-Shemesh and other localities, confirming its role as a strategically important border city.

sens: City in the territory of Issachar in Canaan, near Jezreel
H3694.detail: Kesulloth is a small city allocated to the tribe of Issachar during the division of the promised land (Joshua 19:18). Its name means "sides" in Hebrew, likely referring to its location on the slopes of a hill or mountain range. It is located in the Jezreel region, in the heart of Galilee, and is also known as "Chisloth-Tabor," suggesting a location near Mount Tabor.
H3694.origine: The name Kesulloth comes from the Hebrew kesel, which means "side" or "flank." This same word is used literally to refer to the sides of the body or the sides of an object in other biblical texts. The suffix -oth indicates the plural, hence "the sides." The variant "Chisloth-Tabor" combines the same word with Tabor, the famous mountain of Galilee.
H3694.emploi: Kesulloth appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:18, in the description of the lot assigned to Issachar during the division of Canaan under Joshua. It is mentioned among a series of cities marking the boundaries of this tribe's territory, between Jezreel and Shunem.
