This enumeration situates the city in the fertile plain of Jezreel, a strategic region in the northern center of Palestine. Although little known otherwise, it is an important geographical landmark for delineating the tribal territory.

sens: people descended from Mizraim (Egypt)
ancestors of the Philistines
H3695.detail:
1. The Casluhim are a people or tribe descended from Mizraim, ancient Egypt. They appear in the genealogy of nations listed in chapter 10 of Genesis, where they are enumerated among other peoples that came out of Egypt, alongside the Ludim, the Anamim, and other groups (Genesis 10:14).
2. The biblical text attributes particular importance to the Casluhim: they are the ones who fathered the Philistines, the enemy people of Israel who will dominate the coastline of Canaan and play a major role in the history of the Hebrew people. It is "from whom the Philistines came" according to the biblical expression (Genesis 10:14; 1 Chronicles 1:12).
H3695.origine: The name Casluhim means "fortified" or "fortresses." It reflects an etymology that evokes solidity and defensive capability, which aligns well with the warrior reputation of the Philistines, their descendants. This people appears in ancient genealogies as one of the branches of Mizraim, thus linking the Philistines to Egypt rather than to other Mediterranean origins.
H3695.emploi: The Casluhim are mentioned only twice in the Bible: in Genesis 10:14 and in 1 Chronicles 1:12, in two identical genealogical lists drawn up to establish the origins of the nations after the Flood. Their sole function in the biblical text is to explain the ancestry of the Philistines. Although they play no narrative role themselves, their mention historicizes and connects the Philistine people — whom the Israelites will continually confront — to a legitimate branch of the descendants of Noah's sons, integrated into the geography of the ancient known world.
H3695.portee: This name reminds us that even the historical enemies of Israel, like the Philistines, were part of the order created by God and in the universal genealogy of peoples. For the biblical reader, this underscores divine providence: the nations that arise are never foreign to God's plan.

sens: City of Issachar located on the slopes of Mount Tabor
H3696.detail: Chisloth-Tabor is a locality of the tribe of Issachar, situated on the slopes of Mount Tabor, a well-known mountain in the Promised Land. Its name literally means "the slopes of Tabor," which precisely evokes its geographical position at the edge of this major mountain. It is mentioned during the allocation of land among the tribes of Israel.
H3696.origine: The Hebrew name means "slopes" or "hillsides" (kisalôt) and "Tabor" (the mountain). Mount Tabor was a reference mountain in Palestinian geography, famous notably for the theophany and the events that took place there. Chisloth-Tabor also bears the alternative name Chesulloth, two forms of the same place.
H3696.emploi: Chisloth-Tabor appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:12, at the time when the cities allocated to the tribe of Issachar are enumerated during the conquest of Canaan. It is a border locality, serving as a territorial landmark to delineate the inheritance of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.

sens: To cut, shorten hair by cutting it cleanly
To shave or trim the beard and hair according to a rule
To maintain one's appearance with regular haircuts
H3697.detail:
1. The verb means to cut, shorten by separating a part from a whole with a sharp instrument — here, the hair or beard. It is the concrete action of snipping, cutting cleanly, as one would do with scissors or a razor.

2. In Ezekiel 44:20, the priests of the temple must "cut" their hair: this is an obligation of propriety and discipline for the ministers of worship. This shows that the word designates an action of personal maintenance, a regular and neat haircut, neither shaved nor neglected.
H3697.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a primitive root that denotes the action of separating, dividing by cutting. The word evokes the image of sharpness, the gesture that separates and orders. It fits within the vocabulary of hygiene and personal appearance in Israel.
H3697.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 44:20, to regulate the appearance of the temple priests. It expresses a command regarding the maintenance of hair and beard: neither shaved nor unkempt, a proper measure between these two extremes. This liturgical context shows that the personal appearance of the ministers of worship is important in God's eyes.
H3697.portee: This ordinance reveals that God cares about order and discipline, even in matters of outward appearance. For the believer, it invites sobriety and self-respect in the maintenance of one's body, a sign of an ordered and consecrated inner life.

sens: Cereal resembling wheat, cultivated in the fall or spring
Grain that is sown and harvested like other crops
H3698.detail:
1. Spelt is an ancient cereal, a close relative of wheat, but distinct from it. It is recognized by its particular grain, enveloped in a tougher husk. It is sown and harvested in the appropriate seasons, like other crops: it is therefore part of the stock of food grains known and used in Israel.
2. In Exodus 9:32, spelt and wheat were not struck by hail because they are "late" — that is, they grow later in the season and were therefore not yet sprouted at the time of the plague. In Ezekiel 4:9, the prophet must make bread mixed with several grains including spelt, to signify famine and scarcity: this grain thus figures among the basic food resources of the people.
H3698.origine: The Hebrew word "kussèmet" belongs to the vocabulary of cereals and agricultural crops. It specifically designates a variety of rustic wheat, suited to various climates and seasons. In the Bible, it is found alongside other grains such as barley, wheat, and millet, all essential to the life of the farming people.
H3698.emploi: The word "spelt" appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 9:32, during the plagues of Egypt, it marks a distinction: while hail destroys some early crops, spelt and wheat, being later, are spared. In Isaiah 28:25, it is among the grains that the wise farmer sows in its proper place, in good order. In Ezekiel 4:9, in the sign of famine, it is part of the composition of a distress bread where several grains are mixed: it is a humble and nourishing grain, testifying to scarcity and subsistence reduced to the most varied and basic resources.
H3698.portee: Spelt shows us how the Bible anchors its revelation in the concrete and agricultural world of its readers. This grain also reminds us that God knows the cycles of seasons, crops, and the daily life of the people: He does not speak from above, but engages with the real farmer. For the believer, this affirms that nothing that nourishes man is foreign to Him.

sens: Evaluate the number or quantity of something
Estimate a share or portion based on a given criterion
H3699.detail:
1. To count primarily means to evaluate the number or quantity. In Exodus 12:4, at the time of Passover, the Israelites must "count" for the lamb: they calculate how many people will participate in the meal and choose the lamb based on this count.
2. The word also takes on a sense of estimation or distribution: it involves setting a portion, a share according to what is edible. It is a practical calculation, a judgment on the suitable quantity — less abstract than a simple mathematical count.
H3699.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root expressing the idea of counting, enumerating, or making calculations. It is infrequent in biblical Hebrew. Its use in a rationing context (Exodus 12) shows that it refers not only to the counting of people but to the practical evaluation of the sufficient quantity to feed them.
H3699.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Exodus 12:4). It is used to express the practical necessity of adapting the size of the Passover lamb to the number and appetite of the guests. This context reveals that "counting" here does not simply mean enumerating, but evaluating, estimating a quantity with a view to a concrete action — feeding the group gathered for the feast.
H3699.portee: This word reminds us that obedience to God involves a measure of practical common sense. During Passover, the Israelites were not to waste or neglect: they were to count and estimate, that is, exercise thoughtful judgment. For the Christian reader, this illustrates that faith acts with intelligence and responsibility in material matters.
